items.title: Show HN: PS2 games statically recompiled to WebAssembly
items.summary: Article URL: https://github.com/snuri00/ps2-web-recomp Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50052251 Points: 9 # Comments: 0
items.content:
PlayStation 2 games running in the browser without an emulator. The game's Emotion Engine machine code is translated ahead of time into C++, compiled to WebAssembly, and linked against a reimplementation of the PS2's operating system and hardware that draws with WebGPU.

This is the sibling of psp-web-recomp and follows the same method. The first title brought up this way is Gran Turismo 4, chosen because it is one of the most demanding games on the system: it leans on both vector units, on exact floating point behaviour for its replays and license tests, and on graphics tricks that read rendered images back as palettes. It plays from boot through the opening movie, the menus and races, with music and sound effects, and saves to a memory card kept in the browser. A race runs at full speed, 50 frames per second for this PAL release, in Chrome on a laptop's integrated GPU at twice the PS2's resolution, which is how the recording above was made.

God of War II followed through the same scripts. It needed no game-specific code, but it found two bugs that Gran Turismo 4 had never triggered, one in the recompiler and one in the vector unit timing, and a few missing pieces of the PS2's input/output processor. It now plays from the menus through its cutscenes into combat, and holds 60 frames per second in heavy combat at the PS2's resolution in Chrome. At twice the resolution it runs at 48 to 60, limited by the laptop's integrated GPU.

No game data is included here. You bring a disc image of a game you own, and the scripts in this repository turn it into a web page on your machine.

Recompilation. eerecomp reads the game's executable, follows its control flow to find the functions and emits C++ for them in units of 16 KiB of guest code. The output keeps the R5900's quirks: 128-bit registers and the multimedia instructions that work on them, branch delay slots, the PS2's floating point unit, which has no infinities or denormals and rounds differently from IEEE, and vector unit 0 used as a coprocessor. Jumps between units become tail calls, and a thread switch unwinds the host stack and resumes at the guest address, so the generated code never needs a stack per guest thread.

A small PS2 kernel. The EE side of the operating system is answered by high-level emulation: threads, semaphores, interrupt handlers for the DMA controller and the vertical blank, alarms, and the SIF channel that connects the main CPU to the I/O processor. The I/O processor runs the game's own IRX modules, the sound driver, the disc streaming code and the controller and memory card drivers that ship on the disc, on an interpreter of its R3000 CPU, while the IOP kernel and the libraries those modules call are reimplemented in C++. The disc is read over HTTP Range requests, so only the executable is downloaded up front.

Vector units. Most of a PS2 game's 3D work happens in microprograms the game uploads to vector unit 1. They run with bit-exact PS2 float math and with the pipeline delays of the MAC, status and clip flags modelled, because games schedule their code around them. Microprograms seen during a test run are compiled ahead of time into SIMD C++; any the page meets for the first time are translated into a WebAssembly module on the spot, which takes a few milliseconds per program.

Graphics. The Graphics Synthesizer's 4 MB of video memory lives on the GPU, in its native swizzled layouts, and drawing is done by WebGPU compute shaders: triangles are binned into tiles and rasterized with the GS's own rules for texturing, palettes, alpha blending, depth and destination alpha tests. Because everything stays in GS memory, effects that render into a texture or reinterpret a framebuffer as a palette work the way they do on the console. The internal resolution can be one, two or three times the native one. A software rasterizer of the same GS remains as the reference the GPU output is compared against.

Threads. The emulation runs in a worker, vector unit 1 has a worker of its own the way it runs in parallel on the console, and the GS commands go through a ring buffer to the page thread, which owns the WebGPU device.

Sound and movies. The SPU2 is reimplemented with its 48 voices of ADPCM, ADSR envelopes and the streaming DMA games use for music, and its output goes to an AudioWorklet through shared memory. Movies are decoded by an implementation of the IPU, the PS2's MPEG-2 decoder.

The first race ran at 3 frames per second natively, with a software rasterizer and an interpreter for vector unit 1. Moving the GS to WebGPU compute shaders and compiling the vector unit programs brought it to about 70 natively, and most of the remaining work was about where the browser spent its time rather than the emulation.

The first version of the GPU renderer submitted around 650 compute dispatches per frame, because every texture upload and palette load split the batch of triangles around it. Hoisting uploads ahead of the triangles that do not depend on them, with the same output, brought that to about 80.

Gran Turismo 4 uploads the same 3 MB of textures every frame of a race. GS memory is swapped between frames, so the uploads cannot simply be skipped, but a 16 MB cache of recently uploaded contents on the GPU lets most of them be served without crossing from WebAssembly to the GPU again, which cut the data sent per frame by about 60 percent.

At three times the native resolution the frame rate dropped to 23. Profiling the shader showed that the per-triangle setup was being loaded after a branch that differed between threads, which made the whole setup divergent, and that uploads split into 1 MB pieces blocked Chrome's page thread. Loading the setup uniformly and writing each frame's data in one piece brought three times the resolution to 48 to 50 frames per second on the same integrated GPU.

The browser's own scheduling mattered too. Nested setTimeout calls are clamped to 4 ms, so the emulation loop now yields through a MessageChannel instead, and moving the emulation into a worker, so that the page thread only feeds the GPU, steadied a race that had wandered between 40 and 50 frames per second at a constant 50.

God of War II went from an ISO to a page through port.sh with only generic changes, and each one was a bug or gap that the first game had simply not exercised.

It started with silence. The game's sound driver drives its tick from one of the I/O processor's hardware timers, which nothing had implemented, so the driver never mixed a sample. The intro after the difficulty menu was a mess of huge flat polygons, and when the gameplay was about to begin the game crashed after its render list ran past the end of memory and overwrote its own vertical blank handlers. Following a corrupted linked list back with hardware watchpoints led to the recompiler: when a branch was the last instruction of a 16 KiB unit, the path that does not take the branch continued in the next unit at the delay slot instead of after it, running that instruction twice, or running the instruction a branch-likely should have skipped. That fixed the crash and the game reached combat, still with giant polygons over parts of the screen. Those came from triangles that should have been culled. God of War II's microcode reads the clip flags three instructions after the CLIP that sets them, and the vector unit model made them visible only after four, which Gran Turismo 4, whose microcode always waits longer, could not have noticed.

Along the way it also needed a boot path like the BIOS gives, a module loaded from memory instead of the disc, and the scratchpad DMA's destination chain mode.

You need git, CMake, Ninja, a C++20 compiler (clang is preferred and picked up automatically), Python 3, and 7-Zip if your disc image is in a .7z . Everything has been run on Linux on x86-64. The first run installs the Emscripten SDK into tools/emsdk , or uses the one EMSDK points to, and downloads wgpu-native for the headless test runner. Expect about 300 MB of disk space per game for the generated code and the builds; the disc image itself is linked, not copied.

port.sh takes a disc image (an ISO, or a ZIP or 7z archive holding one) and does the whole job. It reads the boot program named in the disc's SYSTEM.CNF , translates its machine code to C++, and then runs the game headless a few times. Static analysis cannot see every function a game reaches through pointers, so each run writes down the addresses it could not find, the script adds them as entry points and translates again, until a run gets through without new ones. The same runs record the vector unit microprograms the game uploads, which are compiled ahead of time as well. Last it builds the page into build/web-mygame . God of War II goes from ISO to page in three and a half minutes on an 8-core laptop.

The exploring runs press start and then cross every five seconds, which gets most games through their title screens, and put an empty memory card in slot 1 the way the page does, so they follow the path a player takes. --press 900:cross replaces that with your own inputs and --frames sets how long each run lasts. Frames from the last run land in games/mygame/shots , which is the quickest way to see how far a new game gets. scripts/build_web.sh mygame rebuilds only the page.

items.title: Postgres isn't slow, your storage is
items.summary: Article URL: https://clickhouse.com/blog/posette-talk-recap-postgres-isnt-slow-your-storage-is Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50052163 Points: 57 # Comments: 31
items.content:
At POSETTE 2026 , Sai Srirampur presented "Postgres Isn’t Slow. Your Storage Is." a talk examining how storage affects PostgreSQL performance at scale. This post recaps the benchmark, what the results revealed, and the architecture proposed for running PostgreSQL on local NVMe in production. You can watch the full talk in the video linked below.

The talk starts with several symptoms teams running Postgres at scale may recognize: ingestion slows down, P95 read latency becomes unpredictable, autovacuum falls behind, checkpoints compete with your actual workload for resources, or logical replication accumulates lag. These problems do not always share the same cause, but they can have a common one that is easy to overlook: storage performance.

To understand why, Sai ran a benchmark comparing the same 3.3-billion-row PostgreSQL workload on baseline gp3 EBS and local NVMe. We will walk through the setup and what Sai discovered when analyzing the results, then close with the production patterns proposed for running Postgres on local NVMe.

There are five common issues that often appear once a PostgreSQL workload reaches hundreds of gigabytes or terabytes and is running with real concurrency and throughput.

Slow ingestion. The first one is ingestion pipelines heavy on UPDATEs and UPSERTs. Jobs that once finished in seconds can stretch into minutes as the volume of data underneath them grows.

Inconsistent read latency. Next one appears in workloads where most queries remain fast but a few become dramatically slower. P95 latency moves from milliseconds to seconds, dashboards time out, and the uneven slowdown makes the cause harder to isolate.

VACUUM falling behind. A third issue is autovacuum falling behind as UPDATE and UPSERT throughput grows, with table bloat accumulating from gigabytes into terabytes.

Slower checkpoints. Checkpoints can also take longer and compete with the client workload for I/O and CPU, turning an operation that used to be invisible into a recurring latency spike.

Logical replication lag. The last symptom appears when PostgreSQL data is streaming to systems such as Kafka or ClickHouse. WAL decoding can be slow and a growing replication slot can compound the problem.

As the working set outgrows the memory available to PostgreSQL and the operating-system page cache, more data read require physical I/O. On slower storage, the higher cost and queuing of those reads can increase both average and tail latency.

Client queries and background maintenance also use the same storage budget. Heap and index writes, WAL synchronization, checkpoints, VACUUM, and logical-decoding spills compete for bandwidth, IOPS, and queue capacity.

Once storage reaches one of those limits, operations begin delaying one another. That is how slow storage can be the root cause of several apparently unrelated PostgreSQL problems.

The case for local NVMe is not that it eliminates I/O, but that it can sharply reduce its cost. The comparison contrasts millisecond-scale operations on network-attached storage with operations that may complete in tens of microseconds on local NVMe. Cache misses, WAL flushes, and maintenance I/O still happen, but they simply don’t impact the overall system as much.

To better understand why this is the case, Sai set up a simple experiment to compare a similar workload on PostgreSQL running on EBS and local NVMe.

To isolate storage as the variable, the benchmark used eight identical PostgreSQL clusters: four using instance-store NVMe and four using baseline gp3 EBS provisioned at 3,000 IOPS. Each cluster ran on an m6id.4xlarge instance with 16 vCPUs, 64 GiB of RAM, and 16 GiB of shared_buffers. We used multiple instances for each storage type to normalize variability across benchmark runs.

The setup used a 482 GiB pgbench_accounts heap containing 3.3 billion rows. Each cluster then ran the same highly concurrent random-UPDATE workload for five minutes, with 64 clients and 16 worker threads:

In short, the only difference between the two groups was the storage class.

The benchmark produced a median 16,030 TPS for the NVMe clusters, compared with 1,734 TPS on EBS—a 9.24× difference in this test. Median transaction latency fell from 36.9 ms to 4.0 ms.

For different operations, NVMe completed a VACUUM over 10 GB of bloat in 366 seconds, compared with 964 seconds on EBS, and drained a 10 GB logical-replication backlog in 139 seconds instead of 238 seconds.

One qualification matters: these results apply to this workload and these storage configurations. The EBS side used baseline gp3 provisioned at 3,000 IOPS, different EBS setup would most likely produce different results.

The throughput gap becomes easier to understand by looking at where the 37 ms of EBS transaction latency went.

In this benchmark, page reads accounted for about 19 ms on EBS, compared with 0.3 ms on NVMe. WAL fsync at commit added another 11 ms on EBS versus 1.5 ms on NVMe, while lock and scheduler overhead contributed about 5 ms versus 0.2 ms. CPU work itself was roughly the same—about 2 ms in both cases.

In other words, most of the additional EBS latency came from waiting on storage, not from PostgreSQL doing more CPU work.

A mid-run pg_stat_activity snapshot showed the same pattern from another angle. Of the 64 backends, 29 on EBS were waiting on IO:DataFileRead , compared with nine on NVMe—roughly 45% versus 14%. This was a point-in-time snapshot rather than an average across the run, but it illustrates how many more EBS sessions were stalled on reads at that moment.

The CPU profile then adds a counterintuitive observation. Over a profiling window of roughly 240 seconds, the NVMe host accumulated 2,253 CPU-seconds—about 9.4 cores busy—while the EBS host accumulated only 251 CPU-seconds, or about one core busy. Some PostgreSQL functions appeared proportionally hotter on EBS, but the absolute CPU time showed that EBS processes were spending far more time off-CPU waiting for storage.

The NVMe host kept more of its CPU capacity busy doing useful work. That helps explain the much higher throughput: cache misses, WAL flushes, and maintenance I/O still occurred, but they completed faster and left PostgreSQL spending less time blocked on storage.

After the performance results, the talk turns to the obvious objection: instance-store NVMe is tied to the lifetime of a machine, so the local data disappears with the node. The operational question is whether PostgreSQL can combine NVMe latency with production-grade availability and recovery.

The short answer is yes, given durability is provided at the cluster level rather than by any individual Postgres node.

Running PostgreSQL on local NVMe in production means designing around storage that is fast but tied to the lifetime of a machine. Losing a node means losing its local copy of the data; instance-store volumes cannot be snapshotted through the EBS API; and available capacity depends on the selected instance type.

The production architecture presented in the talk addresses this through three main requirements: replicate the database so the service can survive node loss, maintain backups and recovery data outside the individual machines, and plan capacity around the NVMe available on each instance type. Together, these patterns make it possible to run NVMe-backed PostgreSQL confidently in production.

The first pattern is quorum-based synchronous replication with two standby candidates. With a configuration such as ANY 1 (standby1, standby2) , a transaction can commit after either standby durably acknowledges its WAL rather than waiting for the slower of the two. Placing the nodes across availability zones protects against an AZ failure.

For durability outside the database nodes, open-source tools such as WAL-G can provide physical base backups and continuous WAL archiving. With low-latency WAL shipping, this architecture can target an RPO measured in seconds and support point-in-time recovery within the retention window.

Backups and WAL should also be kept in a separate failure domain, with another regional copy when the recovery plan needs to survive a full regional outage.

Base backups and archived WAL are more than an emergency mechanism: the same recovery history can support point-in-time restores, isolated branches, deployment resizing, read-replica seeding, and disaster recovery.

Backups and replication solve different problems. In the architecture described in the talk, standbys provide rapid failover, while backups protect against corruption, operator error, and cluster-wide failure; both recovery paths need regular testing.

This pattern is not only theoretical, the talk cites public examples from Instacart, which has described PostgreSQL on NVMe for a latency-sensitive search workload, and Datadog, which has discussed local-NVMe PostgreSQL instances for workloads that need them. The recurring pattern is local storage for performance, synchronous replication for availability, and independently stored base backups and WAL archives for recovery.

The talk closes with a diagnostic suggestion: when PostgreSQL appears to stop scaling, inspect the database and storage together. Slow ingestion, unpredictable read latency, vacuum pressure, disruptive checkpoints, and replication lag can be signals that the storage layer has reached a limit.

items.title: Ft: 'Mosca vuole uccidere i vertici della difesa europea'
items.summary: Italia ridimensiona, ma in Polonia Tusk annuncia arresto del suo potenziale attentatore
items.content:
Nel gergo dell'intelligence russa è noto come 'wet work', espressione che indica operazioni violente, in particolare omicidi su commissione, con dinamiche addirittura simili a usi della più spiccia criminalità. Operazioni che però adesso rischiano di essere più frequenti e quasi a fare da 'danno collaterale' al conflitto in corso in Ucraina, se è vero - come scrive il Financial Times - che l'allarme è alto tra gli 007 occidentali sull'intensificarsi di sforzi per assassinare i responsabili della difesa europei. Allarme che ha spinto le aziende ad aumentare le misure di sicurezza attorno ai propri dirigenti di alto livello.

La coincidenza vuole intanto che proprio nelle scorse ore il primo ministro polacco Donald Tusk abbia dichiarato che un uomo accusato di aver minacciato un attentato contro di lui e il suo ministro della Difesa è stato arrestato. Questo a poche ore una riunione di emergenza a Varsavia proprio per far fronte alle notizie già giunte su questa minaccia. Non è stata ancora chiarita la provenienza delle minacce, nè è stata resa nota l'identità dell'uomo: il portavoce dell'intelligence polacca Jacek Dobrzynski, citato dalla Tass, ha precisato che Tusk e il suo ministro hanno ricevuto le minacce nelle prime ore del mattino dell'11 ottobre e il quotidiano Gazeta Wyborcza aveva riferito in precedenza che l'avvertimento era giunte tramite canali elettronici.

Peraltro, lo scorso agosto la polizia polacca aveva fermato un 23enne accusato di aver invocato l'assassinio di esponenti politici polacchi di alto livello. E nel 2024 Tusk dichiarò di aver ricevuto minacce dopo l'attentato al primo ministro slovacco Robert Fico. Sta di fatto che la Polonia è un paese Nato al confine con l'Ucraina e i conflitto alle sue porte lo rende un territorio particolarmente esposto a rischi di varia natura.

Il Finacial Times fa intanto riferimento ad assassinii di obiettivi civili europei, un tempo considerati un tabù persino dalle agenzie di spionaggio russe, ma che adesso stanno assumendo un ruolo sempre più rilevante: in sostanza i Ceo e altri dipendenti di alto livello come obiettivi degli agenti del Cremlino, secondo le indicazioni raccolte dal giornale dopo aver sentito funzionari di 5 diverse agenzie di intelligence.

Nel mirino anche i dirigenti delle aziende più piccole, soprattutto quelli delle imprese impegnate nella produzione di droni o dei loro componenti. Così il servizio di intelligence interna tedesco, il Bundesamt für Verfassungsschutz (BfV), ha intensificato notevolmente i contatti con il "personale e i dirigenti" delle aziende tedesche del settore della difesa, arrivando a raccomandare di ricorrere a squadre private di protezione, ha detto una delle fonti. Più in generale, diversi dirigenti del settore della difesa hanno dichiarato al Financial Times di aver rafforzato le proprie misure di protezione negli ultimi sei mesi su specifica raccomandazione dei servizi governativi di sicurezza.

"Dal punto di vista russo, l'obiettivo principale resta psicologico", ha comunque dichiarato un funzionario dell'intelligence. "È sufficiente far credere che potrebbero diventare un bersaglio per ottenere l'effetto voluto: che ci pensino due volte prima di fare affari con l'Ucraina". L'allarme al momento non sembra riguardare direttamente l'Italia: secondo fonti informate che l'ANSA ha potuto contattare, nessun allarme specifico su quanto riportato dal Financial Times riguardo a piani della Russia di assassinare responsabili della sicurezza europei è mai giunto su qualsivoglia canale di comunicazione tra Stati. Quanto descritto dal quotidiano, rilevano le stesse fonti, è frutto di generici alert su possibili scenari che dall'avvio del conflitto in Ucraina non sono mai stati sottovalutati.

items.title: Pixel Watch 5 e Google Health in prova: come va l’allenatore IA al polso
items.summary: Chip più rapido, memoria doppia e GPS rivisto, ma schermo, dimensioni e autonomia dichiarata restano quelli del Watch 4. Le novità vere sono nell'app Google Health e nel suo Coach basato sull'IA di Gemini ... Leggi tutto
items.content:
Questa recensione del Pixel Watch 5 finirà per parlare più di un'app che di un orologio, perché all’esterno il nuovo smartwatch di Google è identico al Pixel Watch 4 dell'anno scorso, con le stesse dimensioni, lo stesso display, anche se c’è un nuovo materiale per il cinturino .

È vero che dentro cambiano il processore, la memoria, e il modo in cui viene elaborato il segnale GPS , ma quello che modifica davvero l’esperienza nell'uso quotidiano è Google Health , l'app che raccoglie i dati di salute collezionati dall'orologio durante il giorno (e la notte) e che propone un coach per l'allenamento (e non solo) basato su Gemini e le analisi mensili della funzione Health Guardian . C’è però da dire subito che nessuna delle due novità è un'esclusiva del Pixel Watch 5.

Stiamo usando il Pixel Watch 5 da 45 mm da metà agosto, associato a un Pixel 11, e mentre scriviamo questa recensione lo abbiamo ancora al polso. La pubblicazione delle recensione è infatti slittata proprio per aspettare le funzioni Health Guardian, che Google ha reso disponibili a fine settembre nell'app Google Health per i Pixel Watch 3, 4 e 5 .

Si tratta di analisi che, a partire dai dati raccolti dall'orologio, restituiscono ogni mese una tendenza della pressione sanguigna, dell'insulino-resistenza e della qualità della respirazione nel sonno. Per quanto riguarda la pressione è importante precisare che non si hanno misurazioni in mmHg ( come negli smartwatch Huawei della serie D ), infatti le analisi Health Guardian sono tutte indicazioni di benessere generale.

Le due taglie sono le stesse del modello precedente, 41 e 45 mm, con uno spessore di 12,3 mm e un peso di 31 e 36,7 grammi senza cinturino. Anche il display non cambia. È un AMOLED LTPO, quella tecnologia che permette di abbassare la frequenza di aggiornamento fino a 1 Hz quando l'immagine è ferma e di risalire a 60 Hz durante lo scorrimento, con una densità di 320 ppi e una luminosità massima dichiarata di 3.000 nit, Google lo chiama Actua 360 e lo protegge con un Gorilla Glass 5 bombato, già visto sul Watch 4.

Splendido alla luce diretta del forte sole estivo e con una luminosità gestita in modo ottimo anche negli ambienti in penombra.

La cassa è in alluminio riciclato, resistente all'acqua fino a 5 ATM, (cioè alla pressione che si trova a 50 metri di profondità), e certificata IP68 contro polvere e immersione.

Le differenze esterne sono tutte estetiche, con le nuove colorazioni Fog e Olive, quest'ultima con cassa color Pyrite, e la Canyon riservata alla versione da 41 mm.

Nella confezione c’è un cinturino sportivo di seconda generazione (la sezione “bucata” ha due unità di lunghezze differenti) che cambia nel materiale: HNBR, una gomma nitrilica idrogenata con finitura “soft-touch”, al posto di quello in fluoroelastomero del Watch 4.

Rispetto all'NBR, l’HNBR (che ha doppi legami della catena saturati con idrogeno) resiste meglio al calore e all'invecchiamento. Ha anche buone proprietà meccaniche, resiste bene all'abrasione e a oli e grassi. Soprattutto non appartiene alla famiglia dei polimeri fluorurati che oggi è sotto scrutinio ambientale per il tema PFAS. È comunque lo stesso materiale che viene usato anche sui Galaxy Watch a partire dalla serie 7.

Il Watch 5 usa lo Snapdragon W5 Gen 2 Accelerated di Qualcomm, una versione rivista del chip del Watch 4, che comunque è sempre affiancato da un coprocessore Cortex-M55 che gestisce le attività in background a basso consumo. Sulla carta una CPU più veloce del 12% e prestazioni complessive superiori del 20% rispetto al modello precedente .

La spazio di archiviazione è passato da 32 a 64 GB e la RAM è aumenta del 50%, quindi dai 2 GB del Watch 4 si è arrivati a 3 GB .

La batteria cresce di poco, da 325 a 332 mAh nel 41 mm e da 455 a 465 mAh nel 45 mm. I valori dichiarati sono identici a quelli del Watch 4, fino a 30 e 40 ore con il display sempre attivo, che salgono a 48 e 72 ore con il risparmio energetico.

Il GPS è sempre quello a doppia frequenza, cioè riceve i segnali satellitari su due bande diverse per correggere gli errori dovuti ai riflessi sugli edifici, ma Google ha rivisto l'elaborazione della posizione dichiarando una precisione fino a due volte superiore nei contesti difficili , come le strade strette tra palazzi alti. Ne parleremo più avanti.

L'elenco dei sensori per la salute coincide con quello del Watch 4. Ci sono frequenza cardiaca, ECG, saturazione dell'ossigeno nel sangue e temperatura cutanea, oltre al sensore cEDA, che misura le variazioni dell'attività elettrica della pelle legate allo stress. Le nuove analisi di Google Health lavorano quindi su dati che anche il modello precedente raccoglie, e infatti Google le ha distribuite anche sui Watch 3 e 4.

Non cambia nemmeno la connettività, con versione LTE opzionale, Bluetooth 6.0, Wi-Fi, NFC per i pagamenti e UWB, la banda ultralarga usata per la localizzazione di precisione. Sui modelli LTE di entrambe le generazioni è disponibile in Italia anche l'SOS via satellite. Per associare il Watch 5 serve però uno smartphone con Android 12 o successivo. Un altro dato che spesso viene dimenticato per questo tipo di dispositivi: il Pixel Watch 5 riceverà 3 anni di aggiornamenti del sistema operativo e delle patch di sicurezza.

Poiché gli anni scorsi i Pixel Watch hanno fatto discutere circa la loro riparabilità, diciamo che batteria e display del Watch 5 si possono sostituire, come sul Watch 4 , che è stato il primo per cui Google ha previsto la riparazione di questi componenti. Uno schermo rotto per una caduta resta comunque fuori garanzia e richiede un preventivo.

Siamo sempre di fronte all’esperienza WearOS (Wear OS 7, che Google distribuisce anche sul Watch 4), e quella data dal Pixel Watch 5 è stata impeccabile dal punto di vista della velocità. Sempre rapido (non rapidissimo) e agile nell’uso di tutti i giorni.

Molte funzioni presentate insieme al nuovo orologio sono arrivate anche sul modello precedente con l'aggiornamento di settembre: i gesti con la mano estesi a Maps, Wallet e agli allenamenti, le informazioni contestuali sul quadrante (non in Italia) e l'attivazione di Gemini sollevando il polso, che ora dovrebbe essere più precisa ma che invece a noi ha smesso di funzionare dopo un po’.

Nello specifico, quando solleviamo il polso compare la mezzaluna azzurra sul fondo, ma se proviamo a parlare all’assistente non otteniamo alcun tipo di risposta è la mezzaluna sparisce. Non siamo più riusciti a farlo funzionare anche riavviando l’orologio.

Come per gli smartphone, anche nel Pixel Watch 5 ci sono però funzioni dipendenti dal mercato o dalla lingua. Gemini offline, che esegue alcune azioni di base come impostare un timer o cambiare un'impostazione anche senza connessione, richiede per esempio la lingua dell'app Gemini impostata in inglese.

Un’altra funzione annunciata con il Watch 5 ma non utilizzabile in Italia è quella dei suggerimenti proattivi di Gemini, ricavati da Messaggi, Gmail e Calendar.

Tornando all’uso vero e proprio, segnaliamo che quando ci si toglie l’orologio e lo si rimette non compare subito la schermata del pin ma il quadrante, quindi bisogna toccare una volta lo schermo per fare apparire il tastierino. Una piccola noia.

Ci sarebbe piaciuto inoltre che all’arrivo di una notifica con lo schermo spento, sollevando il polso ci venisse subito mostrata , invece compare la piccola icona circolare dell’app da premere con un dito.

Infine, due parole sul l’altoparlante del Pixel Watch 5 che è un po’ “a radiolina”. Di contro il microfono fa il suo dovere perché l e telefonate gestite al polso hanno solitamente trovato un buon riscontro negli ascoltatori.

Per quanto riguarda l’autonomia , nella nostra prova (ricordiamo, il modello da 45 mm), con il display sempre attivo e l'orologio al polso anche di notte, il Watch 5 è andato oltre il dato dichiarato .

Al primo ciclo è sceso dal 100 al 20% in 48 ore. Al secondo, che comprendeva anche un allenamento di forza di circa 25 minuti e un'uscita in bici di 35, è arrivato all'10% dopo 52 ore. Un comportamento comunque tenuto costantemente durante i mesi.

Come abbiamo detto, recensire il Pixel Watch 5 è un’occasione per provare anche la nuova app Google Health, che è strettamente legata all’universo Google Pixel e FitBit , perché mette a disposizione tutte le funzioni su tutti gli orologi di Google dalla prima generazione, e accoglie completamente i vecchi FitBit Charge, Versa, Sense e Inspire fino al nuovo Fitbit Air.

Gli altri orologi o fitband di terze parti , come Galaxy Watch, Garmin, Apple Watch, Oura, Amazfit, Xiaomi, si collegano solo come sorgenti di dati tramite Health Connect su Android (o Apple Salute su iPhone). Quindi arrivano passi, distanza, calorie, sonno, frequenza cardiaca e peso, ma Google avverte che non tutte le metriche sono disponibili perché dipende da cosa condivide l'app del produttore .

Come ormai una buona parte delle app di salute o fitness, anche Google Health ha una sottoscrizione Premium da 9,99 euro al meso o 99 euro all’anno . Chi compra il Pixel Watch 5 sul Google Store italiano riceve tre mesi gratuiti. Per sintetizzare subito diciamo che senza Premium resta tutto il tracciamento, la consultazione dei dati e anche Health Guardian che avvisa sulle tendenze della pressione sanguigna, dell’insulino-resistenza, e la qualità della respirazione durante il sonno.

items.title: Copernicus, nel 2026 il secondo settembre più caldo mai registrato
items.summary: Secondo mese nel 2026 che supera di 1,5 °C i livelli preindustriali
items.content: Settembre 2026 è stato il secondo settembre più caldo mai registrato (dopo il 2023) e il secondo mese consecutivo del 2026 in cui le temperature globali hanno superato di 1,5 gradi quelle dei livelli preindustriali. La temperatura superficiale del mare media di settembre per la fascia compresa tra 60 gradi S e 60 gradi N è stata la più alta mai registrata per quel mese, in un contesto di rafforzamento delle condizioni di El Niño. Lo rende noto Copernicus, il servizio meteo della Ue. A settembre le temperature globali hanno raggiunto 1,63 gradi al di sopra del livello preindustriale, proseguendo una nuova serie di mesi iniziata ad agosto con valori superiori a 1,5 gradi, che dovrebbe protrarsi fino al 2027. Le condizioni di El Niño hanno continuato a rafforzarsi nel Pacifico equatoriale, determinando probabilmente uno degli eventi El Niño più intensi mai registrati. Nel frattempo, intorno all'Antartide, l'estensione del ghiaccio marino ha raggiunto il terzo minimo storico per il massimo invernale annuale. La temperatura media globale dell'aria superficiale nel settembre 2026 è stata di 16,27 gradi, ovvero 0,82 gradi al di sopra della media del periodo 1991-2020, ed è quindi risultato essere il secondo settembre più caldo a livello globale, di 0,11 gradi più fresco rispetto a settembre 2023. Il mese di settembre 2026 è stato di 1,63 gradi superiore alla media stimata del periodo preindustriale 1850-1900. E' la prima volta dal novembre 2025 in cui due mesi consecutivi hanno registrato valori superiori di 1,5 gradi.

items.title: Donald Trump sacrifica l’Ucraina facendo un regalo a Vladimir Putin
items.summary: Il presidente statunitense ha concluso un accordo con quello russo sul gasolio e ha attaccato Volodymyr Zelenskyj. Ha poi annunciato una tregua tra Russia e Ucraina, ma Kiev sa che non può fidarsi Leggi
items.content:
Ancora una volta Donald Trump ha pugnalato l’Ucraina alle spalle, stavolta nella speranza di non perdere le elezioni di metà mandato in programma negli Stati Uniti fra tre settimane.

I leader ucraini sentono di essere caduti in una trappola, com’era già successo all’epoca del famigerato incontro fra Trump e Volodymyr Zelenskyj nello studio ovale della Casa Bianca, l’anno scorso. L’ultimo tranello ha distrutto quel minimo di fiducia che era stata ricostruita tra il presidente ucraino e gli Stati Uniti.

All’atto pratico Trump ha fatto un regalo a Vladimir Putin, che riceverà centinaia di milioni di dollari grazie a un accordo con Washington per la vendita del gasolio. Trump addossa all’Ucraina non solo la responsabilità della mancanza di un negoziato tra Kiev e Mosca, ma anche la colpa dell’aumento dei prezzi dell’energia, arrivando a chiedere la sostituzione di Zelenskyj alla guida dell’Ucraina. Si tratta di un’ingerenza palese negli affari di un paese sovrano.

L’11 ottobre Trump ha cercato di correggere il tiro annunciando un accordo tra russi e ucraini per sospendere ogni attacco contro le infrastrutture energetiche, ma è stato immediatamente smentito da Zelenskyj.

La spiegazione di questa crisi è duplice. Da un lato, naturalmente, c’è la risaputa accondiscendenza di Trump nei confronti di Putin, causata in parte dal sogno di concludere grandi accordi economici, ovvero il motore dell’attuale politica estera statunitense.

Dall’altro lato, invece, c’è il ginepraio in cui Trump si è cacciato con la fatidica decisione di attaccare l’Iran, scatenando una guerra che non riesce a vincere e da cui sembra incapace di tirarsi fuori. Il conflitto, tra l’altro, si è ormai esteso alla penisola arabica, teoricamente sotto protezione statunitense.

Le conseguenze politiche di tutto questo sono considerevoli. Negli Stati Uniti è tornata l’inflazione, con Trump che punta il dito contro l’Ucraina e i suoi droni (usati per colpire le raffinerie russe) pur di non ammettere che i prezzi dell’energia sono schizzati alle stelle dopo l’attacco contro l’Iran dello scorso febbraio.

Questa viltà politica non ha nulla di sorprendente, tranne il fatto che si manifesta a spese degli ucraini proprio nel momento in cui subiscono i peggiori attacchi russi dall’inizio della guerra, quattro anni e mezzo fa.

Trump vuole privare l’Ucraina di una delle sue risposte più efficaci agli attacchi russi, impedendole di attaccare le strutture energetiche in territorio nemico mentre Mosca colpisce tutti i giorni quelle ucraine. Zelenskyj si è detto pronto a un accordo reciproco per sospendere queste operazioni, ma ha bisogno della garanzia di un reale impegno del Cremlino.

Il rischio è che gli Stati Uniti neghino all’Ucraina le informazioni di intelligence di cui ha bisogno per portare avanti la sua guerra, cioè l’aiuto principale che gli statunitensi continuano a fornire a Kiev. In questo senso la tensione fra Trump e Zelenskyj a proposito di un avvicendamento alla guida del paese, preteso dal presidente statunitense, non lascia ben sperare. Zelenskyj ha ricordato a Trump che sono gli ucraini a dover decidere, non lui.

L’Europa ha reagito in ritardo, ma alla fine si è schierata a sostegno di Zelenskyj. Era ora che il continente smettesse di sottomettersi a una Casa Bianca che ha evidentemente perso la testa. Quella a cui stiamo assistendo è una dimostrazione di cinismo di stato da parte di Trump, decisamente più ostile con gli alleati di quanto non lo sia verso gli avversari. D’altronde è un meccanismo che si ripete costantemente fin dal suo ritorno alla Casa Bianca, quasi due anni fa.

items.title: Andy Burnham ha detto che la Russia ha interferito nel referendum sulla Brexit
items.summary: Secondo il primo ministro britannico è chiaro che ci siano state ingerenze russe nel voto
items.content:
Il primo ministro britannico Andy Burnham ha detto che è chiaro che la Russia ha interferito nel referendum per Brexit del 2016. «Quando sono arrivato a Downing Street», ha detto Burnham, riferendosi alla residenza del primo ministro britannico a Londra, «ho posto questa domanda: dunque c’è stata un’ingerenza della Russia nel referendum del 2016? Ho ricevuto una risposta chiara: sì c’è stata».

È la prima volta che un primo ministro britannico conferma che la Russia cercò di influenzare il referendum su Brexit, anche se c’erano da tempo avvertimenti sui tentativi russi di esercitare un’interferenza nella politica del Regno Unito. I precedenti governi conservatori avevano insistito sul fatto che non ci fossero prove di un’interferenza russa sul referendum.

Burnham ha reso pubblica questa informazione durante un’intervista a The Rest Is Politics , il podcast di approfondimento politico più seguito nel Regno Unito. Non ha specificato chi gliel’abbia fornita, né su quali prove si basi e nemmeno se le interferenze russe potrebbero aver alterato il risultato del voto.

«Credo che in realtà su questo aspetto siamo rimasti troppo sulla difensiva» ha detto Burnham «e non abbiamo informato a sufficienza l’opinione pubblica su quanto si stia cercando di destabilizzare il processo politico dall’estero». Nell’intervista il primo ministro ha detto di aver parlato del problema delle interferenze russe anche con il cancelliere tedesco Friedrich Merz durante la sua visita in Germania e ha aggiunto: «C’è certamente disinformazione che dalla Russia si riversa nella politica tedesca».

items.title: Type-safe HTML templating in Zig
items.summary: Article URL: https://lalinsky.com/2026/10/11/type-safe-html-templating-in-zig.html Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50051573 Points: 105 # Comments: 45
items.content:
I’ve done a lot of web development over the years. I started around the year 2000, just after PHP 3.0 was released and started taking over the web world. I’ve used all kinds of approaches for generating HTML: raw PHP, string concatenation in Python, Smarty templates in PHP, Template Toolkit in Perl, and Jinja/Django templates in Python. Then, as the world moved on to SPAs and JavaScript frameworks, I stopped working on frontends.

Two years ago, I picked up Zig, and I’d never have imagined I’d be considering web development in such a low-level language. But as I was building my own ecosystem with zio and Dusty , I realized it’s not that far-fetched. I built these libraries for API backends, where the output is JSON or MessagePack, but then I saw that with proper use of arena allocators, even web development is actually manageable, since you don’t need to remember to deallocate all the strings that are typically involved. And with Zig’s comptime, you can build very high-level interfaces without losing the performance benefits. And with the help of htmx or Datastar , you can even build SPAs without touching JavaScript/TypeScript, which I promised myself I’d never do.

That said, one thing was still missing: templating. String concatenation was not an option, I didn’t want to go back to the pre-2000 CGI days. I had a few requirements for a templating library:

I couldn’t find any solution that would satisfy all these requirements. Then I saw Ziex and I was amazed. It never occurred to me that the JSX approach could be done outside of JavaScript. The developer experience Nurul Huda managed to build in Zig was just unimaginable to me. It didn’t fit my needs directly, because I didn’t want a WASM framework, but the syntax and his approach to integrating Zig code into templates gave me some ideas. Then, after further research, I discovered Templ for Go, and it was pretty obvious to me what I wanted to build.

So, let me present zt (I’m not good at naming, sorry) . It’s an adaptation of Templ to Zig. The templates are parsed and transpiled to Zig code during zig build . That means you can import them directly from your app code, but also, perhaps even more importantly, the templates can import your app code. As a result, all parameters can be fully typed. If something can’t be rendered, the Zig compiler will tell you so. The generated code is fairly simple, all it does is write to a std.Io.Writer . You can write directly to a socket or accumulate the output in a buffer, your choice. Here is what a template looks like:

If you want to use it inside Dusty to render an HTML page, you just do this:

As a side note, the main snippet above has a very non-obvious bug in error handling if you use the same pattern somewhere std.Io cancellation matters. I’ll probably write a blog post about it, but if you are interested, check out this Ziggit thread . The render function in Dusty that wraps the std.Io.Writer handling solves it.

All dynamic values are HTML-escaped by default, both in text and in attributes, and values in URL attributes like href or src are also checked for dangerous schemes. If you really need to output raw HTML, you have to ask for it explicitly with {!value} , so it’s easy to spot in the template. The parser also requires all elements to be properly closed, so you can’t accidentally produce broken markup. It won’t protect you from everything, but it removes the most common sources of XSS.

What I like the most is that template errors are just Zig compiler errors. If you make a typo in the template above and write {u.nmae} instead of {u.name} , zig build will tell you:

The error points to the generated code, but each line has a comment with the location in the original template. The same applies to the calling side, if you try to pass a string where HomePage expects a ?User , it won’t compile.

Beyond the basics shown here, you can build reusable components and pass them around as values, and with @children you can build layouts that wrap other templates, which covers what you’d use template inheritance for in other languages. Control flow is just Zig, so if , for and switch work as you’d expect, including payload captures. All of it still compiles down to a sequence of writes, without any allocations.

You can have a look at the TODO example in Dusty. It’s a simple htmx-based web app that showcases this library, plus other parts of Dusty that are needed for building a dynamic SPA.

One part of the syntax is still open. Block-level control flow is written as plain Zig, following the example of Templ, so a line starting with if , for or switch is parsed as code. That means text like “if you forgot your password…” on its own line is a parse error, and you have to wrap it in an element or write it as a string expression. I’m considering switching to @if , @for and @switch , similar to Razor or Twirl, which would remove the ambiguity, at the cost of slightly noisier templates. If you have an opinion on this, please leave a comment in this GitHub issue .

Although multiple people are already using it, the project is not very mature yet, so I welcome any feedback. You can open a GitHub issue if you find any problems, or ping me on the Zig Discord.

items.title: Documents falsified to evade tax on Abramovich's wealth, BBC finds
items.summary: Backdated paperwork also made the Russian oligarch’s yachts and mansions disappear from accounts, investigation finds.
items.content:
The world's biggest accountancy firm helped in falsifying documents to hide Roman Abramovich's wealth and evade tax, BBC Panorama has found.

Accounts signed off by Deloitte in Cyprus meant assets such as superyachts, mansions and private jets worth $672m (£508m) vanished from Abramovich's company accounts.

Deloitte also appears to have advised on a scheme to evade a huge tax bill on the oligarch's wealth through the falsification of documents.

Barrister Andrew Mitchell KC, an expert in financial services law, said Panorama's evidence showed the scheme was "straightforward" tax evasion and "it couldn't be more blatant".

Roman Abramovich's lawyers said he denies that he evaded tax or concealed his fortune. They said Panorama provided no evidence he knew about, authorised or directed the falsification of any document and said it was legitimate to rely on advice from professionals.

Deloitte Cyprus said it "acts in compliance with applicable laws".

The findings are being revealed following a joint investigation between BBC Panorama and the Bureau of Investigative Journalism.

For nearly two decades, Roman Abramovich was the most famous Russian oligarch in the UK, welcomed in London where he bought Chelsea Football Club in 2003 and bankrolled the club's most successful period. But after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, he was sanctioned by the UK government as an associate of President Vladimir Putin and forced to sell the club.

Abramovich has been reported to be living in Turkey, a safe haven for him because it did not apply sanctions. In the Channel Island of Jersey, £5.4bn of his assets remain frozen and a criminal investigation has been going on for four years.

The oligarch's lawyers told the BBC he denies the allegations in the Jersey investigation and says it was "undertaken for political purposes".

Our investigation has uncovered new evidence about the way Abramovich's business empire has been run. It also raises serious questions about the integrity of some of his professional advisers.

The evidence is contained in a leak that includes thousands of documents about the oligarch's finances and the operations of a network of offshore companies administered from Cyprus - which used to be a tax haven popular with Russians - between 1995 and 2022.

The BBC and media partners including the Guardian, Paper Trail Media, the Organised Crime and Corruption Reporting Project, and the Cyprus Investigative Reporting Network - as well as the Bureau of Investigative Journalism , external - have been reporting on the leaked files since 2023 as part of the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists' Cyprus Confidential , external investigation.

In 2022, Panorama also reported on how Abramovich had made his fortune from a corrupt deal to buy a Russian state-owned oil company in the 1990s, selling it back to the government a decade later for billions in profit. He has previously said allegations of corruption in the deal are false.

The profits from Abramovich's oil deals in Russia were funnelled into a web of offshore companies. They were administered from Cyprus by a corporate services firm called MeritServus, in Limassol, the island's second-largest city.

Until 2005, Deloitte - now the biggest of the "big four" firms which dominate the accounting industry - owned MeritServus. After they split, the two companies worked closely together with Abramovich's associates to manage his global fortune.

The leaked documents from MeritServus reveal some of their practices.

He was the Russian oligarch who brought his wealth to the UK. But what’s the truth about Roman Abramovich’s fortune? Panorama investigates the documents that were falsified to hide his wealth and evade tax.

Watch now on BBC iPlayer or on BBC One at 20:00 BST on Monday 12 October.

Our first example of backdated paperwork comes in 2006, after a new law in Cyprus meant that company accounts had to be made public. The new transparency law threatened to expose the secrets of Abramovich's vast wealth.

Deloitte Cyprus had prepared draft accounts for 2003 - but had not yet finalised them - for his Cypriot company Amiscan Investments. The accounts detailed $672m of luxury property.

A mansion in West Sussex, a luxury flat in London and an estate in the south of France were all included - plus helicopters, private jets and a small fleet of boats the oligarch owned at the time, including the $147.5m Pelorus.

To keep them secret, Abramovich's associates and Meritservus decided to rewrite history. They drew up a plan to circumvent the transparency law by transferring the assets to Amiscan's parent company in the British Virgin Islands (BVI), where they could be kept hidden. And they backdated the change by three years to make it look like the asset transfer had happened in 2003.

Deloitte Cyprus reviewed the backdated documents and said they were "adequate" to allow them to remove the assets from Amiscan's accounts.

When the 2003 accounts were signed off by Deloitte in 2006, the homes, planes and yachts disappeared at the stroke of a pen. Only $75,000 of assets remained.

Deloitte signed off the accounts even though the leaked documents show it knew they were completely misleading.

Lord Sikka, professor of accounting at the University of Sheffield, said it was a "violation of a statutory duty" and "pretty scandalous" to misrepresent transaction dates and not to publish true and fair accounts.

Panorama also found evidence that backdated documents had been used in a tax evasion scheme.

This involved another one of Abramovich's Cypriot companies, Kravin Investments, which had almost $2bn in the bank in 2003.

It had been earning large amounts in interest, so Roman Abramovich's company should have been paying tax on that interest to the Cypriot authorities.

An email from MeritServus in August 2005 to Abramovich's Russian associates said a plan had been devised after a meeting with Deloitte. "If you agree, it will be necessary to change the financial statements and the accounting records accordingly for 2003 and 2004," the email read.

MeritServus informed the oligarch's Russian associates, that Kravin's "Provisional Tax Assessments for 2005" would be filed showing the company earning no income from the money.

A month later, an associate in Russia emailed in response, "I agree".

MeritServus then created a series of backdated documents which falsely purported to show that Kravin was only holding and investing the funds on behalf of its parent company in the BVI.

This made it look like Kravin did not actually own the money, so it would not be liable for tax in Cyprus.

Deloitte wrote in a September 2005 email that "certain changes will have to be made to the accounts (bank account balances, interest income, profit and loss account)" because of the backdated changes to Kravin's assets.

So Deloitte was apparently advising on the falsification of financial records. The evidence suggests it allowed Abramovich's company to evade millions in tax.

Andrew Mitchell KC told us the scheme was "straightforward" tax evasion. "If it happened in England and it was in the millions, His Majesty's Revenue and Customs would be thinking about a prosecution," he said.

Cypriot MP Christos Christofides said that if tax had been evaded, then "we have to see how we can get our money back and how, if some people are guilty, they have to pay the price according to our law."

In addition to the documents which Deloitte helped to backdate, Abramovich's advisers at MeritServus falsified a third set of records. This involved the oligarch's huge business fortune - more than $10bn - held by a company called Electus Investments in Cyprus.

MeritServus backdated documents to make it look like Electus did not own the fortune.

It used another Abramovich company with exactly the same name of Electus Investments, but this time based in the more secretive BVI, where accounts did not have to be made public.

Emails show that in 2006, MeritServus acknowledged that the fortune was owned by Electus Cyprus. But again it proposed to rewrite the past, this time "to transfer the beneficial ownership to Electus Investments in the BVI" and make it look as though the change had happened three years earlier.

MeritServus signed and backdated documents which falsely purported to show the BVI company had owned the $10bn fortune since 20 November 2003. So when the accounts of the Cypriot company with the same name were made public, it appeared to have assets worth just $145,000.

Andrew Mitchell KC told Panorama: "What you take away from it is there are professionals who are prepared to bend and break the rules of their profession and therefore the law. And it looks that they will stop literally at nothing in terms of creating documents."

Vladimir Milov, Russia's deputy minister of energy as Abramovich built his empire and now a critic of the Russian government, said: "For each Russian oligarch or Middle Eastern or African corrupt oligarch, there's an army of Western financial and legal services and PR services providers, who is easily taking money for whitewashing their reputation and making them look normal."

items.title: Will Linux phones become a viable alternative to the Android/iOS duopoly?
items.summary: Article URL: https://amosbbatto.wordpress.com/2026/10/05/linux-phones-alternative/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50051530 Points: 137 # Comments: 140
items.content:
by Amos Batto (2026-10-05), License: CC BY 4.0 , Download: PDF , ODT

Five years ago, Linux phones looked like they were poised to become a viable alternative to the Android/iOS duopoly that has an iron grip on the mobile phone industry. Sadly, after a brief flash of activity and community engagement with the release of the Purism Librem 5 and the PINE64 PinePhone in 2020, the Linux phone market has generally stagnated. This stagnation occurred partly because of the problems at Purism and PINE64, but also because the available Linux SoC’s weren’t up to the task of running a modern smartphone, and the hardware industry wasn’t providing any good alternatives with good free/open source drivers. In addition, Plasma Mobile and Phosh were still inchoate mobile interfaces at the time, and there wasn’t a good distro option to run these interfaces on Android kernels with a normal integrated mobile SoC. The poor performance of the PinePhone and Librem 5 and the problems with the PinePhone Pro and the Librem 5 refunds sapped people’s enthusiasm and willingness to take a chance on the next Linux phone.

Fortunately, all of these conditions are changing, and I believe that there is now the possibility that Linux could finally become a viable alternative to Google’s Android and Apple’s iOS in the mobile space, just like desktop Linux has become a viable alternative to Windows and Mac OSX on the PC over the last three decades. This isn’t to say that mobile Linux will fundamentally challenge the business of Google or Apple, but the conditions are ripe for a small market to arise for Linux phones, similar to the way that people can currently buy Linux PCs from a number of small companies, such as TUXEDO , System76 , Purism , Slimbook , ThinkPenguin , Ubuntushop.biz , Entroware , Star Labs , Juno , Laptop with Linux , Linux Certified , ArkPC , etc.

It isn’t impossible that one of the big phone brands might sell a few models of phones with mobile Linux in the future, just like Lenovo and Dell currently sell a few PC models with Linux preinstalled in some limited markets. Motorola just announced that it will start selling some high-end phone models with GrapheneOS in 2027, which indicates that Google will allow the big phone makers to sell alternatives, probably because it fears anti-trust regulation. As the mobile industry increasingly shuts down the ability to unlock the bootloaders of Android phones, more people will be looking for an alternative to AOSP derivatives, and mobile Linux could provide that alternative.

Five years ago, it looked like mobile Linux had finally arrived. The Purism Librem 5 and PINE64 PinePhone had just been released, and even a big tech reviewer like Linus Tech Tips was trying them out . Mrwhosetheboss’s video, “ Are Linux Smartphones about to KILL Android? ,” where he held up the Librem 5, got 7.8 million views on YouTube. The Librem 5 had been ported to Mobian and postmarketOS , and the PinePhone had been ported to 20 different Linux distributions. There was a growing number of phone models that could run Jolla’s Sailfish OS and Ubuntu Touch on top of Android kernels, and many people were testing postmarketOS on their old phones . Plasma Mobile and Phosh were advancing fast as mobile interfaces. KDE had adopted Kirigami and GNOME was adopting Adwaita , so both KDE and GNOME apps could become adaptive between desktop and mobile interfaces. The Waydroid project was making it possible to run Android apps inside a Linux container. The future seemed bright for mobile Linux, but that future never seemed to arrive. It is worth examining what held back mobile Linux to understand how those conditions can be overcome in the future.

There has been great deal of experimentation with different mobile operating systems based on a Linux kernel over the last 25 years since the first mobile Linux devices were released—the Sharp Zaurus , the G.Mate Yopy and the Motorola A760 . I count 29 different varieties of commercial mobile Linux that have existed over the years, and there are probably many more that I missed. There have been many different waves of mobile Linux, which at the time looked like they might become the next big thing, including EZX , MotoMagx , Maemo , LiMo , Moblin , Meego , Tizen , Firefox OS , webOS , Ubuntu Touch and Sailfish OS . For years Motorola experimented with different Linux varieties that were based on the idea of using Java apps available in a community store, so Google’s Android was hardly unique, but it was the flavor of mobile Linux which succeeded. Today, all of them are often lumped together under the label of “Linux” as a separate category from Android, but Tizen and Firefox OS are just as distinct architecturally as Android from a standard desktop Linux distro.

The mobile Linux operating systems live on, although they are less visible today. Much of the MeeGo code that Nokia created for the N9, continues to be developed by the tiny Finnish company, the Jolla Group , which is once again selling phones with its Sailfish OS. Firefox OS, which was abandoned by Mozilla Foundation in 2016, was reborn in 2017 as proprietary KaiOS for low-end phones without touch screens, but that market is slowly disappearing as Android now reaches even the cheapest segments of the mobile phone market. Ubuntu Touch, which was abandoned by Canonical in 2017, lives on as a community-based project under the volunteers at UBports . Even, webOS and Tizen still exist, although they are no longer used as mobile operating systems. webOS runs LG TVs and Tizen is used in Samsung TVs.

Although it doesn’t generate many headlines in the tech press, a tiny Linux phone market still exists. Purism , PINE64 , FuriLabs , Jolla , Jolla-Devices , Volla and PrivacyPortal (plus Brax in the future ) all sell phones with some flavor of Linux preinstalled. The number of people buying Linux phones today is fewer than in 2020-22 when PINE64 was launching the PinePhone and PinePhone Pro, but there are actually more companies selling Linux phones than there was 5 years ago. There are good reasons to believe that many of the problems that plagued Linux phones in the past are going to be overcome in the future.

In the past, the available hardware choices limited the viability of Linux phones. Systems-on-a-Chip (SoC’s) which support Linux are generally used in single-board-computers (SBC’s), TV setup boxes, internet of things (IoT) devices and embedded microprocessors in industrial and automotive applications, where the price points are lower, so their performance is generally weaker and they are less energy efficient than the typical mobile SoC designed for smartphones, because they are fabbed on older process nodes. However, they offer long-term support, because they are used in applications that have long product life cycles. For example, automobiles contain dozens of SoC’s and they typically takes 3 to 5 years just to design and need to be able to run for the next 20 years. In contrast, the mobile SoC’s with Android support are very powerful, but they are only produced for 1 to 3 years.

If the designers of Linux phones want to be able to run a Linux kernel (as opposed to an Android kernel), most of their options offer little processing power, poor energy efficiency and poor thermals. If they want to avoid proprietary blobs as much as possible, they either have to choose an older SoC which the community has been worked on for years to iron out the bugs in the free/open source drivers (e.g., the Allwinner A64 in the PinePhone), or they have to spend years patching the Linux kernel to properly support a newer SoC (as Purism did with the NXP i.MX 8M Quad in the Librem 5). If they decide that it is too much trouble to send their patches to mainline Linux, then it will be harder to support their hardware in the future, because they will have to keep applying those same patches to each new Linux kernel release. Purism chose to upstream their changes to mainline Linux, whereas the volunteers working on the PinePhone’s kernel generally didn’t.

The chipmakers like NXP, Rockchip, Allwinner, Amlogic and Broadcom who make SoC’s with Linux support simply don’t generate enough revenue to justify using a leading-edge process node in their chips. Even thought they can sell a Linux SoC for 10 to 15 years, they still won’t sell enough to recoup the extra $400 – $600 million that it would cost to use a 3nm process, and the costs keep going up with each new generation of process node. It is enormously expensive to design a chip at the cutting edge of the silicon industry. Silicon Analysts estimates that fabbing a wafer at TSMC costs an average of $19,500 at a 3nm node, but only $3000 at a 28nm node. Most Linux SoC’s are low-priced chips with very thin margins, so they have to sell millions of them to make much profit. Some Linux SoC makers like NXP focus on specialty markets, so they they have higher margins, but they tend not to sell many of them, so the profits are still limited.

Another way that chipmakers reduce their costs is by using older generations of Cortex cores, which have lower licensing fees from ARM, and by using lots of low-power Cortex-A5 series cores, rather than the higher-power Cortex-A7 and Cortex-X series cores, which have higher licensing fees. NXP was clearly employing these cost cutting strategies with its i.MX 9 series processors. The most powerful chip in the series is the i.MX 95, which contains six Cortex-A55 cores, when it would have made more sense to use two Cortex-A78 cores for better performance and four Cortex-A55 cores for low power. The i.MX 95 was fabbed on a 16nm FinFET node, which is a slight regression compared to Samsung’s 14nm node used in the previous i.MX 8M Plus processor. Another example of this cost cutting was the decision by Broadcom to use older Cortex cores and larger process nodes in its BCM2836 (40nm, 4x Cortex-A7), BCM2837 (40nm, 4x Cortex-A53), BCM2711 (28nm, 4x Cortex-A72) and BCM2712 (16nm, 4x Cortex-A76), despite knowing that millions of these chips would be sold (e.g. in the Raspberry Pi 2, 3, 4 and 5, respectively). Even Nvidia, which is the world’s richest chipmaker due to the AI boom, appears to be avoiding the costs of using a leading-edge process node in its Tegra SoC. It canceled its planned Tegra Atlan series which was announced in April 2021, and still hasn’t released its Tegra Thor series, which was announced in September 2022. Its Tegra Orin series which was announced in March 2018 is now getting long in the tooth using an 8nm node.

items.title: Il Pato e l'arte di non sentirsi piccoli
items.content:
Roberto Abbondanzieri, detto Pato, oggi ha 54 anni e vive a Bouquet, un paese di circa 1.500 abitanti nella provincia argentina di Santa Fe, dove è nato. Ha investito i soldi guadagnati facendo il calciatore in terreni e macchinari, coltiva soprattutto cereali e soia. È diventato un grande intenditore di mietitrebbie e trattori come suo padre, dopo aver imparato come si usciva sui cross e come si comandava una difesa.

Roberto Abbondanzieri, detto Pato, faceva il portiere, e molte cose si imparano sul mondo guardandolo da una linea di gesso, con la testa sotto una traversa. È diventato un micidiale pararigori, eppure da ragazzino non glieli lasciavano vivere. Se una partita finiva in quel modo, prima di andare a tirarli veniva sostituito. Nel 2003, contro il Milan a Yokohama, il Boca ha vinto l’Intercontinentale perché lui fermò Pirlo e Costacurta. Lo chiamano Pato perché camminava e correva come Daffy Duck della Warner Bros, il Pato Lucas per gli argentini. Fino al 2002 era Abbondancieri, con la c. Il cognome della famiglia italiana era stato trascritto male, e lui ha recuperato la z originaria per ottenere un passaporto europeo.

Oggi ha lasciato il calcio anche se può dirsi l’unico al mondo ad aver attraversato tre ere e diviso il campo con i tre giganti della storia argentina recente: Kempes, Maradona e Messi. C’è un piccolo trucco. Con Kempes ha giocato solo un amichevole omaggio, ma con Diego è stato al Boca, con Leo in Nazionale. Sembra la stessa storia che in Italia ha vissuto Massimo Mauro, compagno di Platini alla Juve, di Zico all’Udinese e di Maradona a Napoli. Solo che Mauro ha concentrato i suoi incontri in una stessa epoca, il Pato ha attraversato le generazioni. Quando però deve scegliere chi sia stato il migliore, fa il nome di Riquelme, sebbene tre anni fa abbia sostenuto la lista avversaria alla sua nelle elezioni del Boca, così come Mauro ha amato Diego ma pensa che Zico sarebbe stato il suo allenatore ideale.

Mauro pare un personaggio de La Terrazza di Scola, Abbondanzieri sembra uscito dalle pagine di García Márquez. Nel vivere una condizione del genere, esiste il rischio doppio di sentirsi da un lato abusivi, dall’altro di complicarsi la vita per dimostrare di essere all’altezza. Bisogna saper stare accanto a un monumento senza passare la giornata a guardarlo dal basso ma senza la tentazione di salire con lui sul piedistallo. È una specie di ricerca di indipendenza. E quando tutto finisce, dopo l’ultima partita, scopri il piacere di essere atteso da un trattore in un campo.

items.title: Columbus Day is about more than Columbus. It’s about Italian Americans
items.summary: For Italians, Columbus is a navigator from a history textbook. For earlier generations of Italian Americans, he was a champion who defended their cause. The celebration is not about a controversial mariner, but about a community
items.content:
“America! We discovered it. We named it. We built it!” This old Italian American saying celebrates Christopher Columbus, Amerigo Vespucci, and the hard work of the six million emigrants who left Italy for the US between the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, labouring in the fields, factories and mines, and in the cities where they settled.

Beneath the tongue-in-cheek boast lies a proud, painful demand recognition and citizenship: “We did all this, and you still treat us as intruders?” Here lies the ethical and identity-based divide between the parade, with its booming drums and banners, along New York’s Fifth Avenue, and our 12 October – in Italy: three caravels in school essays, a postage stamp, marble busts in public squares, surrounded by pigeons.

For Italians, Columbus is a navigator from a history textbook. For earlier generations of Italian Americans, he was a champion who defended their cause. The Genoese explorer, now accused of racism in America, long served as a champion of those discriminated against as “Wops”, the undocumented immigrants reviled with that contemptuous slur.

On 12 October 1492, Columbus lands in the Bahamas in the service of the Spanish crown and becomes to become a symbolic founding father of America. Before Italians embrace him, the young American republic adopts him, eager for a family tree free from the hated British monarchy.

Immigrants from Southern Europe and Latin America then find in the Catholic navigator from Liguria a champion against the hostility of White Anglo-Saxon Protestants (Wasps). The underlying message is: “We were here before you.”

In New Orleans, on 14 March 1891, a drunken mob storms the jail and lynches eleven innocent Italians to avenge police chief David Hennessy, murdered under mysterious circumstances.

The brutality forces Italy to recall its diplomats, while Theodore Roosevelt, the future president, exults: “A very good thing,” convinced that “Italians are worse than Negroes.” In 1892, President Benjamin Harrison proclaims a national holiday to mark the 400th anniversary of the voyage of the Niña, Pinta, and Santa María, a gesture of reconciliation after the massacre.

Italian associations, the Knights of Columbus, of which John Kennedy was a member, and eventually the powerful National Italian American Foundation, NIAF, cement the tradition. The politically astute Franklin D. Roosevelt invokes Columbus from the White House in the 1930s. Bricklayers, dockworkers, mechanics, and families who were learning English from their children march behind an Italian whose greatness America acknowledges, even as that same greatness goes unrecognised in factories and by the police.

John Kennedy embraces this politics of dignity. In Newark, New Jersey, on 12 October 1962, he calls on Americans to remember not only the navigator but also Americans of Italian descent: governors, members of Congress, soldiers and citizens, finally recognised by the first Catholic president.

Before long, however, many come to see an oppressor rather than a liberator in the statue at Columbus Circle in Manhattan. As early as 1977, a conference at the United Nations proposes replacing Columbus Day with Indigenous Peoples’ Day.

In 2020, during the protests following the killing of George Floyd, an unarmed citizen whose life was taken by criminal police officers in Minneapolis, Columbus statues were toppled and mutilated: the statue in Baltimore is thrown into the harbour. Meanwhile, President Donald Trump loses no opportunity to extol the admiral at the White House.

Those who dismiss these protests as “woke” excess, or political correctness, ignore the historical archives, faithful witnesses to the past.

In his letters, Columbus unscrupulously organises the slave trade to Spain. Michele de Cuneo, a companion on the second expedition, recounts in 1495, in a matter-of-fact tone, the deportation of hundreds of Indigenous people and sexual violence against Indigenous women.

In 1500, royal commissioner Francisco de Bobadilla compiles a report detailing brutal abuses. Columbus is arrested on Hispaniola and sent back to Spain in chains, along with his brothers Bartolomeo and Diego. Ferdinand and Isabella release him but do not restore his governorship of the Americas. Bartolomé de las Casas, who arrives in the Caribbean in 1502, records even more horrific cruelties in his History of the Indies . This is therefore not a question of imposing our twenty-first-century sensibilities: Columbus was already reviled by his contemporaries.

In Italy, Columbus never became a figure through whom the nation could achieve a sense of collective redemption. Genoese, yes, but in the service of Spain, he would never become a Garibaldi or a Mazzini.

Genoa celebrates him, schools and monuments preserve his memory, and since 2004 there has even been a national day in his honour. Yet Italians have never needed to rally around his name to feel Italian.

Marching down Fifth Avenue are the descendants of people who were humiliated for being Italian. Honouring them does not require absolving Columbus.

Robert Allegrini, president of NIAF, captures the distinction perceptively: “We proudly support Columbus Day because it celebrates Italian American pride.” The celebration is not about a controversial mariner, but about a long-established, courageous and generous community.
