items.title: All roads lead to Rome. Or do they?
items.summary: A new map of the Roman Empire’s road network charts 300,000 kilometres of routes. Archaeologist Tom Brughmans: “Many of our stereotypes come from looking at the Appian Way. But not every road was straight, and many cities were better connected than the capital.”
items.content:
All roads led to Rome. But also to Antioch, Ankara and Byzantium. “These cities were better connected than the capital of the Roman Empire.”

Another common assumption is that Roman roads were straight and well paved. “But only where geography allowed it, in flatter regions.” When confronted with steep mountains — above all the Alps — the Roman road network departed from the familiar image of smooth, straight highways, despite feats such as the tunnels built in the Aosta Valley.

Tom Brughmans knows this better than most. An archaeologist at Aarhus University in Denmark, he and his colleagues have produced the most comprehensive map yet of the Roman Empire’s road network — and he has personally walked many of those ancient routes.

Contrary to the old saying, at the empire’s height, around the second century, its road network provided easier access to several provincial capitals — including modern-day İzmit, Sofia, Aquileia and Narbonne, and above all Byzantium — than to the Eternal City itself, which was often easier to reach by sea.

You were born in Belgium and teach in Denmark. Why have you devoted your career to the Roman road network?

“Roads tell us a great deal about the people who travelled along them. People, animals, goods and diseases all moved along Roman roads. Legions marched along them. They were used to feed Rome, a city of a million people, with wheat coming from Alexandria in Egypt. It was through these roads that new and revolutionary ideas, such as Christianity, spread.”

“With a series of questions that sound almost like clichés. Did all roads lead to Rome? Were they really straight? Are the roads we travel on today the same ones that existed under the empire? If you start with the Appian Way, all these assumptions seem to be true.

But archaeological excavations today are challenging many of these long-held ideas. And that raises new questions: if not all roads led to Rome, where did they lead? Which cities were best connected? How much did geography determine their routes? To answer those questions, we created the most detailed map yet of the Roman Empire’s road network.”

Your work led to itiner-e.org, an online map of the Roman Empire’s road network.

“I’ve been working on it since 2020 with my colleague Pau de Soto. Archaeology has always focused on the major arteries, such as the Appian Way. We knew very little about the secondary network. We divided up the different regions of the empire and conquered them, so to speak, searching for every source that mentioned roads connecting cities, digitising the newly identified routes and applying network-science methods to the results. We discovered that the Roman road system was twice as extensive as we had thought: 300,000 kilometres, seven times the circumference of the Earth. But we’ve only uncovered the tip of the iceberg. The empire’s road network was even more extensive than that.”

“Between fieldwork and holidays, I’ve walked Roman roads in every part of the empire — Albania, Syria, Spain, Turkey and, of course, Italy. Last summer, my family and I ventured along Hadrian’s Wall. We used Itiner-e to look for the military routes along the frontier. In Rome last year, I decided I would walk everywhere: no buses, no metro.

“Not at all — it’s an extraordinary experience. But it is also the source of some of our stereotypes: that Roman roads were always straight and that all roads led to Rome. The Appian Way fits our idea of the perfect Roman road: paved, straight and heading directly towards Rome. But it is only straight in its first section, in Lazio. After that, it twists and turns like all the others.”

“I’m very fond of the Via Augusta because it tells the story of Rome’s gradual expansion, the difficulties of administering newly acquired territories and the challenge of supplying food to the capital. Southern Spain was one of Rome’s earliest provinces, conquered during the Second Punic War, the war against Hannibal.

The Via Augusta followed the contours of that ancient territory, running from Cádiz to the Pyrenees, where it joined the Via Domitia and continued towards Rome. Great riches travelled along it, from precious metals to olive oil.”

“Travel itineraries, such as the Vicarello Cups and the Peutinger Table, which provided directions for travelling across the empire. We also have milestones and lists of cities and smaller settlements.

Connecting all those points took a great deal of work. We used aerial photographs and satellite imagery, as well as colonial-era maps. In the 19th and 20th centuries, French and British armies used detailed maps of the Middle East that showed the surviving traces of ancient Roman roads.”

Do you agree with Pliny the Elder, who said that Roman engineers, unlike those of earlier civilisations, were primarily concerned with practicality rather than “such examples of useless ostentation as the pyramids”?

“Roman roads were all different. They reflected a constant struggle between the landscape and the technology available at the time. At one extreme you have the Appian Way, straight and paved; at the other, the winding sandy tracks of the Egyptian desert, connecting forts and oases. The beauty of the Roman Empire’s road network lay precisely in that diversity.”

items.title: The lending Dutchman: Rotterdam masterpieces come to Ferrara
items.content:
When a museum abroad closes for renovation, Italy seizes the opportunity. It is happening in Rome, where Palazzo Bonaparte has secured masterpieces by Kandinsky from the Pompidou Centre, which will reopen in 2030. And it is happening in Ferrara, where Palazzo dei Diamanti is displaying, until January 10, some of the most fascinating works from Rotterdam’s Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen, currently empty while undergoing renovation.

On loan from one of Europe’s leading museums — whose collection ranges from Bosch and Rubens to Rothko and Cattelan — are paintings, prints and drawings by masters who revolutionised painting between the late 19th and early 20th centuries, from Millet and Van Gogh to Toulouse-Lautrec and Picasso.

Sandra Kisters, the Rotterdam museum’s head of collections, has made the works available for the Ferrara exhibition.

An inspired and highly successful decision was to bring Vasilij Gusella, head of Ferrara’s civic museums, on board alongside the Dutch curator, who has complemented the works from Rotterdam with a selection by Italian artists drawn from outstanding collections.

These include Pescara’s Museo dell’Ottocento, a remarkable showcase for the Barbizon painters and others; the Istituto Matteucci in Viareggio, a leading centre for the Macchiaioli; and the Museo Boldini, one of the jewels of Ferrara’s cultural scene.

The exhibition succeeds in showing that, at the same time as the European art market was discovering the French Impressionists or marvelling at Kandinsky’s spiritual theories, the work of their Italian contemporaries was no less interesting or revolutionary.

Giuseppe Palizzi’s In the Forest of Fontainebleau , painted in 1865 not far from Paris, more than holds its own alongside Claude Monet’s Poppy Field , painted more than a decade later. Boldini’s bridges over the Seine, meanwhile, have nothing to envy in Bonnard’s.

The Italian artists who chose to plunge into the vibrant world of fin-de-siècle Paris experienced that exhilarating period not as outsiders but as protagonists. The exhibition in Ferrara provides ample proof.

The journey through Palazzo dei Diamanti makes this web of relationships particularly clear, without reducing the comparison to a story of Italian artists chasing French models.

The section devoted to the Macchiaioli shows how an independent artistic language had already developed in Tuscany by the early 1860s, based on the synthesis of light and a direct relationship with reality.

A striking example is Telemaco Signorini’s The Honeymoon , painted between 1862 and 1863 and on loan from the Istituto Matteucci in Viareggio. In its unusually elongated format, two figures immersed in the landscape become an almost suspended episode, constructed through contrasts of light and shade and an atmospheric sensitivity that anticipates concerns destined to become central to European painting in the decades that followed.

It is not simply a sentimental interlude, but evidence of how the Macchiaioli technique could transform the observation of reality into a modern form of storytelling.

Divided into nine sections and comprising more than 120 works, the exhibition traces this gradual liberation of painting from naturalistic representation. From the Barbizon school and Impressionism, it moves through Post-Impressionism and Symbolism, the Italian experiments of Divisionism and Futurism, and finally to the dissolution of form in Mondrian and Kandinsky.

The exhibition’s greatest achievement, then, is to avoid telling art history through separate national compartments. French, Dutch and Italian artists are presented as protagonists in the same European laboratory, shaped by travel, exchanges, exhibitions and mutual influences.

What emerges is a less predictable account of modernism, one in which Italy, too, regains its place on the international stage. And the works themselves make the case immediately apparent.

items.title: Un’influenza diversa dalle altre
items.summary: Secondo gli esperti, arriverà in anticipo e sarà dominata da un virus con una mutazione che bisognerà monitorare con attenzione Leggi
items.content:
Secondo gli ultimi dati disponibili, la stagione influenzale nell’emisfero settentrionale sarebbe partita in anticipo, una notizia che potrebbe spingere le autorità sanitarie dei vari paesi a modificare i calendari per le campagne vaccinali. Nel Regno Unito e lungo la costa occidentale degli Stati Uniti la percentuale di persone risultate positive ai test per l’influenza è insolitamente alta per questo periodo dell’anno. In Giappone i focolai registrati ad agosto e all’inizio di settembre hanno portato alla chiusura di alcune scuole in concomitanza con la riapertura dopo le vacanze estive.

“Se la tendenza che abbiamo osservato lungo la costa occidentale degli Stati Uniti sarà confermata, dovremo prendere atto che la stagione influenzale è stata incredibilmente prematura”, spiega Scott Hensley, virologo dell’università della Pennsylvania a Philadelphia.

Negli Stati Uniti il sottotipo rilevato nella maggior parte dei casi è l’H1n1, mentre la stagione precedente era stata dominata dall’H3n2. I dati di sequenziamento ricavati dai primi casi evidenziano la diffusione di una mutazione nell’H1n1 che sta suscitando una certa preoccupazione tra gli esperti.

Dato che questi dati fanno riferimento a un numero relativamente ridotto di campioni positivi rispetto a quelli disponibili durante il picco della stagione influenzale, è ancora presto per fare previsioni. “Un inizio precoce non significa necessariamente una stagione più intensa”, spiega James Hay, epidemiologo dell’università di Oxford, nel Regno Unito. Ma “c’è qualcosa che non torna”, ha scritto l’epidemiologa Caitlin Rivers, ricercatrice della Johns Hopkins university a Baltimora, nel Maryland, nella sua newsletter del 27 settembre, intitolata Force of infection .

I primi dati sono bastati a convincere Rivers a modificare la sua strategia personale d’immunizzazione. In un anno normale, quando la stagione influenzale raggiunge il picco tra dicembre e gennaio, la ricercatrice aspetta fino metà ottobre per fare il vaccino, in modo da massimizzare la protezione. Ma quest’anno ha deciso di farlo in anticipo.

Di solito l’influenza è causata da una combinazione di tre virus: due sottotipi dell’influenza A, H3n2 e H1n1, e influenza B. Dato che i virus influenzali mutano geneticamente nel corso del tempo e l’immunità delle persone cambia in seguito a contagi e vaccini, è impossibile prevedere quale virus dominerà una determinata stagione. In base ai dati raccolti negli Stati Uniti, nella settimana che si è conclusa il 26 settembre l’H1n1 rappresentava il 96 per cento dei casi positivi, mentre l’H3n2 sfiorava il 4 per cento e il virus dell’influenza B non era stato rilevato.

Si tratta di un grande cambiamento rispetto all’anno scorso, quando era emersa una nuova variante dell’H3n2 chiamata subclade K. La variante era diventata dominante a livello globale perché aveva delle mutazioni che rendevano le persone più vulnerabili al contagio.

Quest’anno la mutazione dell’H1n1 che preoccupa i ricercatori è la G155e. Alex Greninger, virologo dell’università di Washington a Seattle, riferisce che il suo laboratorio ha riscontrato la presenza della G155e in 13 dei 17 campioni in cui le sequenze genetiche erano abbastanza complete da poter identificare le mutazioni. I campioni erano stati raccolti nei mesi precedenti negli ospedali e nelle cliniche di Seattle.

Questa mutazione era già stata evidenziata in uno studio condotto da Jesse Bloom, virologo del Fred Hutchinson cancer center di Seattle, pubblicato il mese scorso sul server di prestampe bioRxiv, prima della revisione paritaria ( peer review ).

Bloom e i suoi colleghi hanno analizzato la capacità degli anticorpi presenti nei campioni di sangue prelevati a 260 persone in Australia e negli Stati Uniti di riconoscere e bloccare il contagio da 148 virus dell’influenza A che circolavano alla metà del 2026. “È emerso che vari ceppi in cui è presente la mutazione G155e sono più difficili da riconoscere per gli anticorpi preesistenti”, spiega Bloom. Gli anticorpi prelevati da adolescenti e giovani adulti erano particolarmente inadatti a riconoscere la variante, probabilmente perché molte persone in questa fascia d’età non erano mai state esposte a virus H1n1 con caratteristiche simili.

L’analisi, insieme ai primi dati di sequenziamento provenienti dal laboratorio di Greninger, suggerisce che la stagione influenzale potrebbe essere relativamente più grave a causa di ceppi in grado di sfuggire all’immunità, afferma Bloom.

Ogni anno la composizione dei vaccini contro l’influenza viene stabilita in base alle mutazioni genetiche, con l’obiettivo di proteggere la popolazione contro i virus che hanno una maggiore probabilità di circolare nei mesi successivi. Tuttavia, queste decisioni sono prese con mesi d’anticipo, mentre i virus continuano a mutare. Questo significa che piuttosto spesso, al momento della somministrazione, i vaccini non combaciano con i ceppi in circolazione. L’anno scorso, per esempio, il vaccino non teneva conto della subclade K dell’H3n2, emersa intorno alla metà del 2025, cioè quasi tre mesi dopo la decisione sulla composizione del vaccino per l’emisfero settentrionale.

Quest’anno le componenti del vaccino per contrastare l’H3n2 e l’influenza B sembrano adatte ai virus in circolazione, spiega Hensley. Per quanto riguarda l’H1n1, invece, se i ceppi con la mutazione G155e dovessero diventare dominanti, il vaccino potrebbe non essere particolarmente efficace, sottolinea Bloom, precisando però che è troppo presto per trarre conclusioni.

In ogni caso Hensley aggiunge che per tutti è importante fare il vaccino, che è in grado di assicurare un buon grado di protezione anche quando non è perfettamente allineato con i virus in circolazione. Il vaccino dell’anno scorso, nonostante la scarsa corrispondenza con i ceppi dominanti, si era comunque dimostrato capace di riconoscere il virus H3n2, garantendo una discreta efficacia.

items.title: La povertà silenziosa dei bambini giapponesi
items.summary: Anche se è percepito come un paese dalla ricchezza diffusa, il Giappone ha sacche di povertà relativa che per l’inflazione si stanno allargando. E a farne le spese sono soprattutto i più piccoli Leggi
items.content:
Poco prima di mezzogiorno, nell’afa appiccicosa dell’estate, bambine e bambini cominciano ad arrivare alla spicciolata in una biblioteca di Miyoshi, una città del Giappone centrale. Consegnano i loro buoni e ritirano i bentō , i contenitori con un pranzo pronto. Alcuni si fermano a mangiare al fresco con gli amici, altri portano il pranzo a casa.

Durante le vacanze estive, quando le scuole erano chiuse, la città ha distribuito ogni giorno centinaia di pasti in undici strutture pubbliche. Quella scena tranquilla nascondeva però una realtà ben più cupa. Senza le mense scolastiche o le aule climatizzate durante la lunga pausa estiva, molti di quei bambini avrebbero avuto difficoltà a mangiare in modo adeguato o a trovare riparo dal caldo.

Il Giappone è spesso considerato una società ricca. Eppure al suo interno presenta disuguaglianze a tratti sorprendenti. Secondo i dati del governo, nel 2024 l’11 per cento dei bambini viveva in condizioni di povertà relativa: il reddito disponibile della famiglia, corretto in base al numero dei componenti, era cioè inferiore alla metà del valore mediano nazionale, pari a 2,77 milioni di yen (15.250 euro).

Questo tasso di “povertà relativa” è sceso rispetto al picco del 16 per cento registrato nel 2012. Ma con l’uscita del Giappone da decenni di deflazione l’aumento dei prezzi colpisce duramente le famiglie povere. Dal 2020 i prezzi dei generi alimentari sono aumentati di circa il 30 per cento. Il problema “non è mai apparso così grave come oggi”, afferma Koji Ogawa di Usnova, un’organizzazione non profit che ha contribuito al programma di Miyoshi.

Gran parte del problema deriva dalle particolari difficoltà che devono affrontare le madri sole. Il tasso di povertà relativa delle famiglie monoparentali in Giappone è tra i più alti dei paesi dell’Ocse, per lo più ricchi, e si attesta al 44,7 per cento. E questo anche se quasi il 90 per cento delle madri sole lavora. Il Giappone ha inoltre uno dei divari retributivi di genere più ampi tra i paesi ricchi. Le donne si concentrano nella fascia più bassa di un mercato del lavoro a doppio binario, occupando posti di lavoro “irregolari”, caratterizzati da salari bassi e scarse tutele.

Ad aggravare il problema c’è lo scarso contributo degli ex mariti. In quasi nove divorzi su dieci i figli sono affidati alle madri, ma secondo un’indagine ufficiale il 70 per cento di loro non riceve un assegno di mantenimento. Ad aprile il governo ha modificato il diritto di famiglia introducendo l’affido condiviso: il Giappone è stato l’ultimo paese del G7 a farlo. Le autorità sperano che i padri che continuano a essere presenti nella vita dei figli siano più propensi a contribuire al loro mantenimento.

La situazione economica sta peggiorando le cose. Secondo un’indagine dell’organizzazione non governativa Save the children Japan, quasi il 90 per cento delle persone che hanno chiesto di ricevere gli aiuti alimentari distribuiti dall’organizzazione ha indicato come causa l’aumento dell’inflazione.

Sakiko Gan dell’università Atomi di Tokyo osserva che nel frattempo la loro spesa media giornaliera per mangiare è scesa sotto i 500 yen a persona (2,8 euro), un livello paragonabile a quello di chi vive in condizioni di povertà assoluta.

In Giappone la povertà si vede raramente in modo evidente. Secondo l’ong britannica Greater change, il paese registra il tasso di persone senza dimora più basso al mondo. Eppure le preoccupazioni per le disuguaglianze sono in crescita. Il termine oya-gacha è entrato nell’uso comune. Unisce la parola giapponese che significa “genitore” a quella che indica un tipo di distributore di giocattoli in capsule: significa che i bambini non possono scegliersi i genitori e che le loro prospettive dipendono in larga misura dalla fortuna.

Ci sono delle forme di sostegno per le famiglie in difficoltà, ma sono del tutto inadeguate, afferma Kanazu Honma, direttrice dell’ong Florence. I genitori soli non possono ricevere sussidi se il loro reddito supera determinate soglie, fissate a livelli irragionevolmente bassi. Questo può disincentivarli dal lavorare più ore.

Destinare più aiuti alle famiglie povere rappresenterebbe un uso migliore delle risorse pubbliche, ma è una scelta politicamente difficile. Anche se il costo della vita è diventato una questione politica di primo piano, il dibattito tende a concentrarsi sul ceto medio in difficoltà. Secondo una stima, solo il 20 per cento circa delle famiglie che avrebbero diritto all’assistenza sociale ne usufruisce effettivamente. Lo stigma sociale impedisce a molte di presentare domanda e, quando lo fanno, spesso sono respinte da funzionari poco disponibili.

Ma mette anche in luce una caratteristica più generale della povertà in Giappone: in larga parte persiste silenziosamente, lontano dallo sguardo dell’opinione pubblica.

Internazionale pubblica ogni settimana una pagina di lettere. Ci piacerebbe sapere cosa pensi di questo articolo. Scrivici a: posta@internazionale.it

items.title: I libri scelti da Internazionale
items.summary: Da Pionieri di una nuova terra di Ernest Haycox a Fame di Choi Jin-young. Le recensioni della stampa straniera Leggi
items.content:
Per più di mezzo secolo i pionieri, come furono impropriamente chiamati gli emigranti che percorrevano le piste dell’Oregon e dell’Ovest, sono stati rappresentati come cavalieri dall’armatura scintillante, impegnati a portare la bandiera della civiltà americana verso terre lontane. I diari dell’epoca mostrano invece che nella grande maggioranza erano uomini e donne impauriti e insoddisfatti, spesso impreparati e male informati, che fuggivano dalle fattorie sommerse dai debiti dell’Illinois e dell’Ohio per affrontare fatiche ancora maggiori. Nel suo ultimo romanzo Ernest Haycox segue uno di questi gruppi quando il lungo viaggio è ormai quasi terminato, dalle strettoie del fiume Columbia alla valle di Bear creek, dove i coloni costruiranno le loro case. A guidarli è Bob Hawn, che vive con Louise, una donna nativa americana, e che prima della fine dell’anno avrà modo di pentirsi della propria generosità. Il romanzo racconta quell’anno nella vita degli uomini e delle donne dell’insediamento di Bear creek: Bob Hawn, che accanto a Louise dimentica rapidamente di aver fatto parte della società dei bianchi; il laborioso Rice Burnett e il ribelle Cal Lockyear. Personaggi che reagiscono in modi molto diversi all’avanzare della civiltà, anche nelle sue forme più rudimentali. Pochi scrittori del West hanno conosciuto quei territori e la loro storia meglio di Haycox. Da anni sognava di scrivere quello che definiva un “romanzo panoramico”. Hoffman Birney, The New York Times (1952)

Cresciuta ad Haiti dalla zia Atie, Sophie ha dodici anni quando raggiunge a New York la madre Martine. Il trasferimento apre una profonda esplorazione dell’identità e del trauma che attraversa diverse generazioni. Sophie vive sulla propria pelle una doppia identità, divisa tra le aspettative legate alle sue origini haitiane e la realtà del nuovo paese. Edwidge Danticat costruisce il romanzo attraverso immagini vivissime, capaci di sostenere il peso delle questioni che affronta. Quando incontriamo Sophie bambina, sua madre è già emigrata negli Stati Uniti e Atie è per lei tutto: disciplina, conforto, protezione. Il padre invece è assente. Scopriremo che Sophie è stata concepita durante uno stupro, origine di un trauma che continua a tormentare Martine. Il peso della tradizione emerge soprattutto nella pratica invasiva con cui le madri controllano la verginità delle figlie. La purezza femminile è considerata indispensabile per l’onore della famiglia, ma questa concezione patriarcale finisce per devastare le donne. Atie cerca rifugio nell’alcol, Martine conduce un’esistenza segnata dal dolore e Sophie, a sua volta traumatizzata, da adulta non riesce a vivere serenamente l’intimità con il marito. Danticat restituisce magnificamente tutte le sfumature del rapporto tra madre e figlia: amore, risentimento, perdono. Respiro, sguardo, memoria è una resa dei conti con ciò che ereditiamo e con i traumi che hanno contribuito a costruire il mondo in cui viviamo. Breanna Burke, The Stanford Daily

Tutte le Avane del cubano Pedro Juan Gutiérrez vivono nella sua memoria: quella brutale e notturna come quella dell’infanzia. Meccanica popolare nasce quasi per caso, quando lo scrittore trova per strada alcuni vecchi numeri dell’omonima rivista di scienza e tecnologia che leggeva da bambino. Li compra e, sessant’anni dopo, qualcosa si risveglia. Questi diciassette racconti attraversano tre decenni di vita cubana, dagli anni cinquanta ai settanta. Gutiérrez lavora con memoria e intuizione: “Prendi un pezzo da qui, un altro da là, e prepari una buona insalata”. Al centro c’è Carlitos, un bambino che cresce tra giochi, amori, incidenti e sconfitte mentre intorno a lui Cuba cambia e si sgretola. È un Gutiérrez diverso da quello della Trilogia sporca dell’Avana (Edizioni e/0 2000). Là dominavano sesso, violenza, rabbia e un linguaggio brutale; qui lo sguardo è più innocente. Anche perché lo scrittore stesso è cambiato: “Se sei furioso, deluso, incazzato con la vita, scrivi con furia, violenza, sporcizia. Se sei più tranquillo, descrivi altre cose”. La rivoluzione rimane sullo sfondo, senza essere nominata direttamente: attraversa la vita di Carlitos più che diventare argomento politico. Paloma Navarro Nicoletti, Gatopardo

La radicale disfunzione del nostro mondo è al centro di Fame , l’audace romanzo di Choi Jin-young, diventato un libro di culto in Corea del Sud. Dam trova il corpo senza vita del suo compagno Gu sulla strada e, invece di consegnarlo alle autorità, decide di mangiarlo. Il romanzo torna poi indietro. Dam e Gu sono cresciuti insieme e si amano fin da prima dell’adolescenza, uniti da un’intimità che rende quasi superflue le parole. Tanto più che nella società in cui vivono comunicare sembra impossibile: il senso di responsabilità e la paura di essere un peso per gli altri li spingono continuamente a reprimere sentimenti e lacrime. Su entrambi grava soprattutto il dovere di produrre. Debiti, sacrifici familiari e necessità di guadagnare trasformano progressivamente i loro corpi in strumenti di lavoro: il valore di una persona finisce per coincidere con quanto riesce a produrre e restituire. Choi costruisce così un’elegia tragica per una generazione cresciuta in una società ferocemente capitalista. Al centro di questo romanzo doloroso rimane la solidarietà tra due persone che rifiutano il mondo costruito intorno a loro. Leah Rachel von Essen, Chicago Review of Books

items.title: Messico colpito da due cicloni, scatta l'allarme
items.summary: Simon sfiora Jalisco, alluvioni in Bassa California
items.content: Il Messico affronta una severa ondata di maltempo. L'uragano Simon, di categoria 4 con venti a 215 km/h, avanza in parallelo a Jalisco senza toccare terra, portando comunque precipitazioni estreme. La Protezione Civile, che ha esteso la zona di sorveglianza fino a Sinaloa, ha dichiarato: "Non abbassiamo la guardia. L'uragano si trova molto vicino alle nostre coste". Le autorità hanno quindi raccomandato la sospensione di tutte le attività lungo il litorale. Nel frattempo in Bassa California i resti del ciclone Rachel hanno generato gravi allagamenti a Ensenada, Mexicali e Tijuana. In quest'ultima città l'acqua ha quasi raggiunto due metri di altezza, obbligando i pompieri a usare i gommoni per mettere in salvo otto persone intrappolate nelle abitazioni. La governatrice Marina del Pilar Ávila ha sospeso le lezioni per lunedì 12 ottobre per facilitare la pulizia delle strade e il ripristino della viabilità urbana.

items.title: Roomba in offerta per tutto ottobre: su irobot.it si parte da 149 euro
items.summary: Dodici modelli scontati fino al 31 ottobre, dai Combo d'ingresso ai Max con la base che lava il rullo. E dall'8 ottobre sei robot in offerta anche su Amazon ... Leggi tutto
items.content:
Per tutto ottobre il negozio online di iRobot mette in offerta 12 modelli dei suoi Roomb a , dal Roomba Combo 105 a 149 euro fino al prestanti Roomba Max 775 Combo con base AutoWash. Da oggi e fino al 31 ottobre, 6 modelli sono scontati anche su Amazon , in qualche caso a un prezzo ancora più basso. Se c'era un momento per smettere di passare l'aspirapolvere e il mocio, è questo.

Dodici voci possono spaventare, ma il listino si legge bene se lo si guarda per famiglie. Salendo di prezzo, il robot si prende in carico lavori che altrimenti resterebbero a noi, come svuotare il contenitore della polvere e lavare i panni sporchi. Scegliere significa anche capire fin dove si vuole delegare.

Quasi tutti i Roomba in offerta sono Combo, cioè aspirano e lavano il pavimento nella stessa passata . Si orientano con ClearView LiDAR , un sensore laser che misura le stanze e ne disegna la mappa. Il robot pulisce così per traiettorie ordinate , sa dove è già passato e nell'app si possono indicare le stanze da pulire.

La differenza vera la fa la base di ricarica. Quella AutoEmpty aspira a sua volta lo sporco raccolto dal robot e lo chiude in un sacchetto AllergenLock da 2,5 litri, che trattiene il 99% di pollini e muffe e va sostituito ogni tre mesi circa. La base AutoWash fa lo stesso lavoro e in più lava e asciuga i panni o il rullo lavapavimenti , così il robot riparte ogni volta pulito.

Un ultimo dato che può aiutare a orientarsi è la potenza di aspirazione. Si misura in pascal (Pa) , l'unità con cui si esprime la depressione creata dal motore: più il numero è alto, più il robot tira su sporco dai tappeti e dalle fughe . Nei modelli in offerta si va dai 7.000 Pa del 105 ai 30.000 Pa delle fasce più alte.

Il prezzo più basso del mese è quello del Roomba Combo 105 , a 149 euro, o 179 euro con base AutoEmpty . Anche il modello d'ingresso

Con pochi euro in più si entra nella nuova generazione. Il Roomba 115 Combo , nero o bianco, costa 169 euro è più piccolo della precedente generazione 105 in ogni dimensione : 24,5 centimetri di lato contro 33,6 e 9,2 di altezza contro 10,4, per appena 2,16 kg. Così si infila sotto più mobili, e intanto aspira con 15.000 Pa . La spazzola laterale pulisce a filo parete e anche il suo panno in microfibra si stacca e si lava. Con una carica copre fino a 84 metri quadrati, cioè un appartamento di medie dimensioni.

Ha la navigazione ClearView LiDAR e per il lavaggio usa un panno in microfibra, bagnato da una micropompa con tre livelli d'acqua da scegliere in base al pavimento. Quando riconosce un tappeto, la funzione Carpet Detect lo evita per non bagnarlo . Dall'app Roomba Home si impostano le routine e si sceglie quali stanze pulire per prime.

È uno dei prodotti di punta dell'offerta, e si capisce perché. Il Roomba 115 Combo con base AutoEmpty costa 219 euro e porta lo svuotamento automatico nella fascia d'ingresso.

Il robot è lo stesso 115 appena visto. La base però cambia l'uso quotidiano: a fine pulizia il Roomba rientra, la base aspira lo sporco dal contenitore e per circa tre mesi non serve toccarlo . Chi ha animali in casa, o chi semplicemente non vuole ritrovarsi ogni sera a svuotare un contenitore pieno di polvere, ha qui il modo più economico di dimenticarsene. È in vendita, nero o bianco, allo stesso prezzo.

Con la serie Plus 400 e 500 arriva la base AutoWash , e con lei un design più basso. I tre modelli sono alti appena 8,35 cm , con un profilo più sottile del 21% rispetto al Plus 505 della generazione precedente. In pratica passano più facilmente sotto letti, divani e mobili bassi, dove la polvere si accumula indisturbata.

Il lavaggio è affidato a due panni rotanti DualClean , che girano a 200 giri al minuto. La tecnologia SmartScrub aumenta la pressione sul pavimento contro lo sporco più ostinato , e quando il robot riconosce un tappeto solleva i panni di un centimetro per non bagnarlo.

Il Roomba Plus 415 Combo + AutoWash costa 349 euro e aspira con 20.000 Pa. Il Roomba Plus 515 Combo + AutoWash sale a 22.000 Pa e costa 399 euro. Entrambi sono disponibili neri o bianchi. Chi cerca la generazione precedente trova invece, sempre con base AutoWash , il Roomba Plus 405 Combo a 299 euro e il Plus 505 Combo a 399 euro.

Il secondo prodotto di punta del mese è il Roomba Plus 575 Combo + AutoWash , a 449 euro. Nero o bianco, conserva lo stesso profilo basso dei fratelli ma alza ogni dato.

L'aspirazione arriva a 25.000 Pa. La navigazione passa a ClearView Pro con PrecisionVision AI , una telecamera che riconosce gli oggetti sul pavimento, come cavi, scarpe e oggetti lasciati in giro, e li aggira invece di trascinarli. Anche la base fa un passo avanti: lava i panni con acqua a 75 °C e li asciuga con aria calda , così non restano umidi nella base fino al giro successivo, evitando muffe e cattivi odori.

Nella fascia alta cambia il modo di lavare, perché al posto dei panni rotanti c'è un rullo PowerSpin che strofina il pavimento con acqua calda a 60 °C e si pulisce da solo mentre lavora , premendo sul pavimento con una forza di 15 newton. Entrambi i modelli aspirano con 30.000 Pa, usano la navigazione ClearView Pro con PrecisionVision AI già vista sul 575 e sono alti 9,95 centimetri.

Il Roomba Plus 615 Combo , a 549 euro in nero, è la scelta di chi vuole il rullo lavapavimenti spendendo meno. La sua base Wash Only lava il rullo a 80 °C e lo asciuga, ma non svuota la polvere , che finisce in un sacchetto da un litro integrato nel robot, sufficiente per circa un mese.

Rispetto al 615 cambia la base, ed è la differenza che si sente di più. La AutoWash svuota la polvere, lava il rullo a 80 °C, lo asciuga con aria a 55 °C e dosa da sola il detergente . Si va avanti fino a 90 giorni senza interventi .

Il Roomba Plus 675 Combo + AutoWash è il terzo prodotto di punta del mese. Costa 599 euro ed è disponibile bianco o nero.

Sul robot la tecnologia PerfectEdge allunga il rullo verso i bordi per arrivare fino al battiscopa , e la spazzola anti-groviglio non resta avvolta dai peli degli animali (ha un meccanismo taglia-peli che li accorcia mentre gira, così non c'è da liberarla a mano con le forbici).

La serie Max è quella pensata per le case più movimentate, con bambini, animali e tanti tappeti. In offerta c'è il Roomba Max 705 Combo + AutoWash , bianco, a 599 euro. Lava con il rullo PowerSpin già visto sui Plus 615 e 675, protetto da una copertura che tiene asciutti i tappeti mentre il robot li attraversa, e aspira con 13.000 Pa e due spazzole in gomma anti-groviglio. La funzione Dirt Detect riconosce le zone più sporche , mentre Carpet Boost alza in automatico la potenza quando il robot sale su un tappeto .

Con PrecisionVision AI il 705 riconosce cavi e calzini, e perfino i bisogni degli animali domestici , e li aggira.

La base AutoWash lava e asciuga il rullo con acqua e aria calde , dosa da sola il detergente e svuota la polvere per 75 giorni.

Chi ha soprattutto tappeti e non ha bisogno del lavaggio può guardare al Roomba Max 715 Vac + AutoEmpty , a 449 euro in nero. È un aspirapolvere puro, con 30.000 Pa , le due spazzole in gomma anti-groviglio, Dirt Detect, Carpet Boost e la base AutoEmpty.

L'ultimo prodotto di punta è il modello più completo dell'offerta. Il Roomba Max 775 Combo + AutoWash costa 699 euro.

Riunisce quello che si è visto fin qui e si presenta come il più complet o. Aspira con 30.000 Pa, ha le due spazzole in gomma, Dirt Detect e Carpet Boost degli altri Max, e lava con il rullo PowerSpin, protetto dalla stessa copertura per i tappeti. La base AutoWash svuota lo sporco fino a tre mesi, lava il rullo a 75 °C, lo asciuga a 50 °C, dosa il detergente e rabbocca l'acqua . La navigazione è ClearView Pro con PrecisionVision AI, come sul 705.

Da oggi, 6 Roomba sono in offerta anche su Amazon, con prezzi in qualche caso più bassi di quelli di irobot.it. Tra questi ci sono le versioni 416, 516 e 576: sono le versioni proposte su Amazon dei Plus 415, 515 e 575, con le stesse caratteristiche tecniche.

items.title: Doory – Open-Source Canva
items.summary: Article URL: https://github.com/shaongitbd/doory Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50049872 Points: 107 # Comments: 37
items.content:
See it in action · Features · Templates · Doory vs Canva · Self-host · FAQ

Doory is a full design editor that runs in your browser. Make posters, social posts, stories, slides, invitations, resumes, thumbnails and business cards: start from a template or a blank page, edit everything, and export to PNG, JPG, SVG, PDF, MP4 or GIF. Every feature is free, nobody needs an account to start, and you can run the whole thing on your own server.

A real, unedited recording: pick a template, rename the band, recolour the dates, add a star, export.

Ten starter templates ship with Doory, each with its own palette, set in open-licensed fonts and fully editable: a gig poster, a wedding invitation, an event story, a sale post, a café flyer, a quote card, a resume, a YouTube thumbnail, a pitch deck and a business card. Add your own in the admin, and browse them all by category, size and orientation.

Canva is a great product. Doory is for people who want the same kind of tool, but free, open and in their own hands.

Open http://localhost:8080 and start designing. The web container serves the app and forwards /api and /ws to the backend, so the browser only ever talks to one address.

A new site starts empty. Add whatever you want once it is running:

React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Fabric.js, Yjs and Zustand in the browser; Django 5, Django REST Framework, Channels and PostgreSQL on the server; Docker Compose with nginx, optional Redis and S3-compatible storage.

Bug reports, ideas and pull requests are welcome. Open an issue to report a bug or suggest a feature. For a security problem, please report it privately through the repository's Security tab instead.

Doory is released under the Attribution Assurance License . You may use, change and redistribute it, including commercially, but you must credit the author : keep the licence and NOTICE with it, and display this credit prominently in the running app:

Doory by Siam, creator and maintainer of Doory — https://github.com/shaongitbd/doory

Third-party software, fonts and content keep their own licences; see THIRD_PARTY.md .

items.title: Local Indexing to reduce tool calling and token usage
items.summary: Article URL: https://tedhaley.ca/pensieve/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50049508 Points: 76 # Comments: 18
items.content:
Press Control+Shift for a glass panel over your documents, folders, git repositories and conversations with coding agents. Search by meaning or by the exact words. Pick a result, tap Control, and choose what to do with it without touching the mouse.

Plain words find what you meant, even when the file never uses them.

Quotes match the phrase exactly. Mix both to rank exact hits by meaning.

Filter to files, code or sessions, a file type, or a folder or repo with in: .

Agents are only as good as the context they're given. Connected over MCP, your coding agent asks Pensieve one question and gets back the few passages that matter, with file and line. It starts on the right code in fewer tool calls.

Illustrative example. In the benchmark below, agents with Pensieve averaged 2.0 tool calls per lookup against 3.4 with grep, and answered after a single call in 82 of 144 runs.

An agent started in a repo sees that repo, its worktrees and its sessions. Name a scope to give it a few repos and a folder of specs.

Agents use the same search you do: by meaning, by the exact identifier, or both, across code, docs and past sessions.

Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or any MCP client, over stdio with pensieve mcp or over HTTP. pensieve integrate connects the agents on your Mac and adds a “search before you grep” block and skills, including optional ones that point you to teammates who know the code.

We gave Claude Code the same code-finding tasks with and without Pensieve: held-out tasks across real repos from 500 to 35,000 files, asked five ways, from plain descriptions to exact names and error messages. With Pensieve it finds more of them, with fewer tool calls, and costs less per lookup in every repo. Each search takes 0.1 to 0.2 seconds.

One search, before any agent: how often the answer is the top result.

Claude Sonnet in Claude Code, measured in four real repos. Pensieve costs less in every repo, and saves the most in the biggest one.

Method: Claude Sonnet run headless through Claude Code. Tasks are generated from the code and graded on the file found. “With Pensieve” is the default agent tool set plus the instructions block from pensieve integrate , measured with Pensieve 0.5.6. Both setups ran the same 72 held-out tasks across four repos (504, 1,783, 2,383 and 34,847 files), twice each, in one batch, because the cost depends on Claude’s prompt cache at the time. These tasks were never used to tune Pensieve. Costs are Claude Code’s reported API costs at list prices. Pensieve used 16% fewer tokens. The “right file, first result” chart uses the same held-out tasks: a single grep wins on exact error messages, and Pensieve wins on everything else. The benchmark scripts are open source in bench/ ; run them on your own repos.

Every repo as a map, with git blame for every line. Ask about any topic and get the people with the most domain knowledge, plus what each teammate has been working on lately. The fastest answer is often a conversation.

Who wrote each area, weighted by the lines that are still there today.

Ask about a topic, not a file, and get the people whose code is most about it.

What each teammate shipped in the last 90 days, and the areas next to your work you haven't explored.

When the people who wrote a part of the codebase are no longer active in it, that knowledge is at risk. Pensieve flags those areas, shows how few people still know them, and who knows them best today.

For every area of a repo: how much of the code was written by people still active there, and how many of them there are.

The active people with the most lines in that area, so you know who to pull in before you change it.

Spot gaps before an incident does. Point your agent at the area to draft the missing docs.

Pensieve watches your folders, repos and agent sessions and re-indexes what changed. Uncommitted edits count, and every worktree is tracked by branch, so your agents never work from stale context.

Indexing and search run locally. You decide what gets indexed, and AI is entirely optional.

An on-device embedding model and a local index in ~/.pensieve . Its server answers only this Mac, not your network or other websites. No account, no cloud service.

Agents, folders, repos and apps each have a switch. Turning one off removes what it indexed.

Password-manager exports, keys, .env files and credentials are never indexed.

Summaries and insights are optional. Pick who writes them, or leave it off:

Paste this into Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Qwen Code, Windsurf or VS Code.

Your files and folders (Documents, Desktop, Downloads and any folder you add), your git repositories including uncommitted changes and worktrees, and your Claude Code, Codex and Qwen Code sessions. Obsidian vaults too, and optionally Apple Notes. Everything is indexed and searched on your Mac.

Without it, a coding agent often greps the repo and reads many whole files to find what matters, and every file it reads costs tokens. With Pensieve connected over MCP, the agent asks one question and gets back the most relevant passages with their file and line, so it starts on the right code in fewer tool calls. In our benchmark that made each lookup 18% cheaper and 21% faster; see the measured results above.

In our benchmark, Claude Code with Pensieve found the right file in 131 of 144 runs, against 123 with grep alone, with 43% fewer tool calls. Each lookup cost 18% less overall, and 6–28% less in each of four repos from 504 to 34,847 files. The benchmark scripts are open source, so you can run them on your own code.

Agents grep by habit. The install prompt runs pensieve integrate recommended , which adds a short “search before you grep” section to the instructions files of Claude Code, Codex and Gemini CLI, plus a search skill and two hooks for Claude Code. You can also switch these on in Settings → Agents. With it, the agent used Pensieve in all 144 runs of our latest benchmark.

Any MCP client. pensieve integrate recommended connects Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Windsurf, Claude Desktop and VS Code for you. Other agents can use pensieve mcp over stdio, or HTTP. Optional skills also suggest which teammates know an area and help plan new code around what already exists.

Pensieve reads git blame and recent commit history for each area of a repo. Areas where most lines were written by people with no recent commits there are flagged, along with how many active people know the area and who among them knows it best.

Your files, code and sessions don't. Indexing and search run on your Mac. Pensieve only downloads its models and checks GitHub for updates, which you can turn off. The exception is if you choose Claude Code or Codex to write optional AI insights; those are labelled Cloud. The built-in model, a local server like LM Studio, or no AI at all keep everything local.

No. Search, agent context, ownership and knowledge gaps all work without one. AI insights are optional: choose the built-in Qwen 3.5 9B, LM Studio, Claude Code, Codex, or leave it off.

Yes. It's free and open source under the MIT license. The code is on GitHub .

The app isn't notarized yet. If macOS blocks it, open System Settings → Privacy & Security and click Open Anyway. You only do this once.

The app needs Apple Silicon. On Linux and Intel Macs, the same prompt installs the backend and the browser visualizer. An Intel Mac also gets the search panel if the Xcode command-line tools are installed.

First run pensieve integrate all --remove to disconnect your agents. Then quit Pensieve, drag it to the Trash, and delete ~/.pensieve , ~/.local/share/uv/tools/pensieve and ~/.local/bin/pensieve . Its models are in ~/.cache/huggingface .

items.title: Iconic Australian band Powderfinger announce first tour in 17 years
items.summary: The band, who announced their reunion last week, say they are "absolutely ecstatic" to be playing together again.
items.content:
Powderfinger, one of Australia's best loved rock bands, has unveiled details of a comeback tour – to take place 17 years after they broke up.

The Brisbane-based group, who confirmed their reunion last week, will kick off with four nights in their home city next September.

They will then play another 14 shows across Cairns, Sydney, Adelaide, Perth and Melbourne, with all gigs to be staged in a "stadium sized big-top" tent.

In a statement on Monday the band said they were "absolutely ecstatic" to be getting together and playing again.

"Over the years there have been tons of suggestions for us to go back on the road but, until now, it never felt quite right or lined up for all of us," they said.

"We have always been so grateful for the continued support from our long-term fans and over the years we've picked up a lot of new ones who have never seen us play."

"People often tell us that our music is connected to their most treasured and joyous memories," they added. "We hope to spread a little more of that joy when we make our way around the country with some of Australia's best established and upcoming talent, and to make some new memories for us all."

The tour schedule of only playing on Friday and Saturday nights is similar to that adopted by Oasis in their world tour last year. No gigs outside of Australia have yet been announced.

Powderfinger released seven studio albums during their career including 2000's Odyssey Number Five which was voted best Australian album of all time by listeners of Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC) music station Triple J in 2011.

That included the single My Happiness, which was voted sixth best Australian song of all time by the same station in 2025. The group's other hits include On My Mind and These Days and Sunsets.

Since the band split, frontman Bernard Fanning has maintained a solo career while bassist John Collins has gone on to open two of Brisbane's largest live music venues.

items.title: Illustration Beyond Proof
items.summary: Article URL: https://terrytao.wordpress.com/2026/10/11/illustration-beyond-proof/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50049133 Points: 64 # Comments: 2
items.content:
[This is a guest post by Kate Stange and Edmund Harriss . This blog post was initially written in a different file format and converted using AI. — T.]

In January a group of mathematicians, historians, artists and educators gathered at the Institut Henri Poincaré (IHP) for a very unusual workshop on mathematical meaning. Our focus for that week, as part of a special trimester on the use of illustration in mathematical research, was to ask: what would it mean for an illustration to be rigorous [1]? We did not anticipate how urgent the surrounding cluster of questions, about the very definitions of human mathematical practice, would seem, just six months later. Our discussions led to an article, written over the summer in the context of the Leiden Declaration [2], and now accepted in the Notices [3]. The past month or two have seen a heartfelt outpouring of viewpoints on what it means to do mathematics as a human being, and what it will mean in the near future. It is evident from the impassioned discussions that being a mathematician has many and varied important meanings. Mathematical illustration, which includes computer graphics and other media that speak to our senses beyond symbolic communication, is one of the activities of a human mathematician that goes beyond proof-writing. Its own struggles as a discipline can perhaps provide some insight into where mathematics can go from here.

We begin with a recap of where we are. Bryna Kra [4] describes the heart of the current problem. Over many years, theorem production has become the most important measure of success. Positions and prizes rest upon it. But it has always been a proxy for something harder to measure: understanding. Deep theorems were scarce and difficult, so they reliably identified deep thought. AI has broken that scarcity. For her, a proof is “a story, a picture, an insight, an explanation.” Silvia De Toffoli and Eamon Duede [5] sharpen this perspective, rejecting the idea that mathematics is a game that machines can now win. The goal of mathematics is not simply a verifiable solution. Mathematics is “a body of knowledge engaged with, interpreted, and digested by a scholarly community,” not a registry of results. Matilde Marcolli [6] goes further: the big theorems were never the point, only a value system the community chose, and choices can be made again. Grant Sanderson [7] asks what that means in practice: how do we give real credit to the other forms that mathematical work and understanding take?

Other forms of knowing have been given credit in the past. Our paper begins with the hand-drawing required in mathematical training at Gaspard Monge’s École Polytechnique in the nineteenth century. At the January workshop, historian Frédéric Brechenmacher made this explicit: “Drawing was knowing.” [8] We trace how that tradition was set aside in the twentieth century, but nevertheless persisted, emerging in part in a more recent debate over the relationship of proof and meaning in mathematics in the 1990s. At that time, in response to an influential paper by Arthur Jaffe and Frank Quinn [9], many mathematicians expressed their thoughts, most famously Bill Thurston. In his now much quoted “On Proof and Progress in Mathematics” [10], he defended his work against Jaffe and Quinn’s criticism. Many of the other responses are also worth reading [11]. The Philosophy of Mathematical Practice [12], the field of De Toffoli and Duede, studies these questions systematically across the community.

Algebraic number starscapes: the complex roots of rational cubic polynomials. The right-hand image is a shader by Steve Trettel; code at shadertoy .

The Illustrating Mathematics community developed from this tradition of drawing and making mathematical objects. It took shape during a semester at ICERM in 2019 and went on to organise the IHP trimester this year [13]. It brings together mathematicians who actively develop images, models, software and experiences of mathematics. A particular focus has been the role illustration plays as a method of research: exploring, not just explaining, mathematics. In the same way that a good proof shows more than just its result, a good illustration does much more than demonstrate a form or pattern.

Our own work in algebraic starscapes [14], including the images above is a modest example (with Steve Trettel, and with Jayadev Athreya, Gabriel Dorfsman-Hopkins and Claudio Gonzalez joining in). The pictures show elaborate structure in the complex roots of rational cubic polynomials. When we moved to using shaders to draw the image (on the right), a naive first draft of the code turned circles into ellipses. But we realized that the unintended distortion revealed an extra dimension of meaningful structure. These pictures show mathematics that has not been explored, rather than explaining what is already known.

Of course, both proof and illustration can mislead, especially in research. The capabilities of LLMs come at a cost. In the case of illustration, their ability to produce code makes illustration more accessible than ever before. Yet by vibecoding, we are now two steps from knowledge: even the creation algorithm itself may not be understood.

In the case of proof, this problem of “digestion” is now centre-stage. This month [15], prompted by Ioannis Tsiokos, GPT-6 Astra found Chair44, the first three-dimensional aperiodic monotile. Tsiokos shared a 61-page paper [16]. He says he understood the intuitive geometric argument but not the mathematics. Chaim Goodman-Strauss then distilled the argument into eight pages [17] built around a diagram of matching arrows that makes the supertile structure visible, giving a classical hierarchical proof of aperiodicity. The illustration of the shape itself (in Tsiokos’ paper) was a critical clue in revealing the key idea.

So returning to our original question, in the face of these problems, how can an illustration be rigorous? In the paper we draw on Valeria Giardino’s account of representations as tools for thought ( Endeavour 42, 2018) [18], which considers an illustration’s affordances: the readings, manipulations and inferences the figure invites. We might choose a stronger definition of affordances: the properties of the illustration that a proof certifies as accurate. Conversely, proofs can show that an apparent property is not an affordance. For example, early images of the Mandelbrot set seemed to show it was disconnected [19], but in a pixelated image a feature thinner than the step between pixels can be missed [20]. Properties such as the number of bulbs of a given size off the main cardioid, on the other hand, can be proved correct, provided the pixel size is small in comparison.

If this addresses the accuracy of an image, what about its engagement or ability to reveal? These are questions without clear answers, but they are not unimportant. They are also the questions that academic art asks of the work of its students, and art has a long-tested method: the “crit”. At the workshop, Jean Schmitt, a professor of art foundations, helped us set up a crit framework we used through the trimester. The crit is a discussion of a work, often presented with minimal introduction, to reveal how it is received by the audience. What are the similarities and differences between that reception and the creator’s intent? This gave a more formal structure to the sort of informal conversations we were already having, and placed the discussions in a communal space. The crit shares something with the style of Gelfand’s Moscow seminar.

Schmitt’s workshop talk [21] drew on Tim Ingold’s idea of thinking through making ( Making , Routledge, 2013) [22], in which form and understanding emerge through the process and in collaboration with the tools and materials available. In the same way Monge’s students were expected to learn through the process of drawing, not by observing the drawings of others. Value and understanding often come as much from the effort of creation, be it illustration or proof, as from viewing that created by others.

These ideas from art make explicit and visible something that has always been implicit in the mathematics community. Being a mathematician is as much about being an excited audience for the work of others as it is about presenting or creating our own research. As a community, we value aesthetics, elegance, and insight, and we have developed these shared values through our interactions. The oversized importance of publication and previously unproven results merely overshadowed these broader values, but people have always been working to find ways to ensure we give credit for them.

Infrastructure to support these broader values has also been growing. The Geometry Labs United network [23] brings together groups in many universities where undergraduates and graduates work with postdocs and faculty, exploring math as research, experimentation and visualisation. This gives a natural space for learning through making proofs, experiments, exposition and illustrations. In many cases the proof can be more contextual, proving the affordances of a specific experiment or illustration. Learning through making also aligns with work in mathematics education. In the final talk of our workshop, Hortensia Soto showed how working with physical materials supports learners’ actions, perceptions and sensations on the way to understanding [24].

items.title: Trump faces growing backlash over plans to import diesel from Russia
items.summary: Both Republican and Democratic lawmakers have criticised the deal, which was announced weeks before the US midterm elections.
items.content:
US President Donald Trump is facing a growing backlash over plans to import diesel from Russia as the Iran war continues to impact global energy prices.

Trump on Friday announced that Russian President Vladimir Putin had agreed to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately "to the American and global marketplace" followed by several other shipments.

That is despite signing legislation to authorise fresh US sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas just weeks ago.

The move has been criticised by some Republican and Democratic lawmakers, who believe the deal violates US laws.

As well as the initial release of 300,000 tonnes of diesel, Trump said Russia would then supply 500,000 tonnes in November and one million more after that.

This would be followed by a further three million tonnes, which would be delivered "within a short period" dependent on the condition of its refineries, which have been attacked by Ukraine during the ongoing war between the two countries.

"Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority," Trump wrote in a Truth Social post.

Russia's Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak confirmed these numbers to Tass, the country's state-owned news agency, saying the export volume could reach three million tonnes per month in future.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has called the deal a gift to Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended".

It is understood the US Treasury is suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports until 7 April as part of the deal, but other assets like those in American banks are still frozen.

A group of seven senators - four Republicans and three Democrats – on Sunday said the deal violated US laws, urging Trump to "reverse course".

"The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians," the lawmakers said.

They added that Congress had "explicitly banned Russian energy imports in 2022 to prevent American dollars from financing Putin's brutal war against Ukraine".

The statement was signed by Republicans Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski, Thom Tillis and John Curtis, as well as Democrats Jeanne Shaheen, Richard Blumenthal and Ron Wyden.

Trump's 'energy ceasefire' claim welcomed by Zelensky but Russia silent

Trump wants to reduce the cost of fuel as the midterms loom - will it work?

Analysis: Trump's shock Russia deal highlights mounting pressure to curb fuel prices

Not everyone is opposed to the deal. Republican Thomas Massie, who has sparred with Trump a number of issues, said the US should lift sanctions on all petroleum products.

Trump's Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News the agreement would work through existing legal channels the US has to help bring prices down and that anyone in Congress who said it would not was wrong.

Global fuel prices have soared since the US-Israel war with Iran began at the end of February, with the fighting severely disrupting supplies of crude oil - a key ingredient in petrol and diesel.

The rising prices have become a key issue for Americans ahead of next month's midterms elections, which will determine if Trump's Republican Party maintains control of Congress.

Polls show a majority of Americans disapprove of his handling of the economy and the war in Iran and he has been searching for ways to ease his party's political pain.

The toll the war is taking has been acutely felt by US agricultural states, which rely heavily on diesel to operate farming machinery and to transport their products to market.

The average diesel price in the US is currently $6.28 (£4.74) a gallon, according to the AAA, down from the record high of $6.53 recorded at the end of September.

Analysts have questioned whether Russia is capable of providing that quantity of diesel and the extent to which doing so will ease prices for American consumers.

The US uses approximately 3.6 million barrels of diesel a day, so even if Russia delivers its promised 300,000 tonnes this month, it amounts to approximately half of the US daily consumption.

It is not only at home that Trump is facing opposition to his diesel deal with Russia. A number of international leaders have criticised it, including Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, who said the US and other allies of Ukraine should focus on ramping up pressure on Russia to end the war.

Meanwhile, Trump announced in Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had reached an "energy ceasefire" but did not give more details. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky welcomed this but there was no response from Moscow.

UK does not support Trump's Russia diesel deal, says Streeting

Trump announces deal for Russian diesel as Zelensky calls it a gift to Putin

items.title: American ranchers wrestle with soaring costs - and their loyalty to Trump
items.summary: Many farmers in states that backed the president say they are being hit from all sides, with the crucial midterm elections just weeks away.
items.content:
Nebraska rancher Yvette Mannon was already having a rough year.

In April, a wildfire destroyed 1,600 grazing acres and 13 miles (21 km) of fence along the ranch she bought in 2002. The ranch is nestled in a corner of Nebraska that's home to rolling green hills under sweeping Midwestern skies, the landscape dotted with grain silos and feedlots alongside fields and fields of bovines.

Mannon's 300 cattle survived the blaze - but the fencing needed to be replaced, and the herd still needed to be fed.

With steel prices at their highest levels in years, heavily affected by tariffs imposed by US President Donald Trump, that meant spending $4.89 a foot - for a total exceeding $300,000.

On top of that, because so much good grazing land had been destroyed, Mannon also needed a tractor out every day delivering hay to her cattle - at a time when diesel prices, spiking due to the Iran War, were up more than 40% from the previous year.

Then in August, the Trump administration announced it would import 300,000 metric tons of duty-free foreign beef in a bid to lower consumer prices. The news hit right before the September-November window when most US calves are weaned and sold.

"So we're 'Buy American', 'Let's Make America Great'," said Mannon, 63, who voted for Trump. "But for you guys over here, sorry."

Many farmers and ranchers across the US say they are being hit from all sides. Recent years have been difficult, with drought affecting crops and already historically low cattle herds. But they say government policies have added to the strain.

That has left some in Nebraska, which overwhelmingly backed President Trump during the last election, reassessing their political allegiances.

Dan Osborn, an independent candidate running against Trump-backed Republican Pete Ricketts, is performing surprisingly well in the polls ahead of November's Senate race.

Republicans seem keenly aware of the discord and frustration among farmers. Both Trump and Nebraska Governor Jim Pillen have in recent weeks announced relief policies aimed at lowering fuel costs for farmers and ranchers, who say they have been struggling for months.

The Iran War has sent diesel and fertiliser prices skyrocketing - both daily necessities for agricultural operations. Tariffs have affected machinery costs and repairs, as well as steel and lumber prices.

And decisions by the Trump administration - whether it be importing foreign beef or opening up the southern border to Mexican cattle - have sent already-volatile markets into overdrive.

Many producers are losing hundreds of dollars per head of cattle.

"All of this hit cattle markets, as a whole, negatively," said James Mitchell, an assistant professor and agricultural economist at the University of Arkansas.

Cattle markets run in 10-12 year cycles, he said, with some good years and some bad. The industry recently enjoyed a particularly lucrative period, where low supply and high demand drove up prices. But now, the market is clearly on a downswing.

Jake Wolfinger, 45, has been weathering the downturn at his feedlot near Lexington, Nebraska. He and his wife are both Ohio natives hailing from multi-generational farming families. They moved to Nebraska - which enjoys lush land and the most groundwater in the nation - to strike out on their own.

The Wolfingers bought a dilapidated feedlot in 2010, which they have turned into a sophisticated operation with 5,500 cattle. Neighbours point to them as an example of what hard work can still do in a tough industry.

But Wolfinger did not factor the Iran War, tariffs or foreign beef imports into his planning.

"Things were just chumming along pretty good," he said, selling cattle for $240 per hundredweight - but that's dropped to $225. That may not seem like much, but it means a loss of potentially hundreds of dollars a head.

Wolfinger is also contending with sky-high diesel costs, with some equipment going through 400-gallon tanks a day.

A Trump supporter, Wolfinger said he voted for the president because "we needed his spirit in this country". He also expressed frustration with what he called "woke DEI" policies on the left.

But he is unhappy with the way the president has intervened in the beef market.

"People need to stay the hell out of farmers' business, because it's harvest time," Wolfinger said.

Forty miles northwest, near Callaway, Nebraska, 54-year-old Duane Kimball stands in his shed surrounded by machinery - and a huge Trump banner along one wall.

"I know a lot of people have had to go back to their banks and increase their lines of credit."

But he does not blame Trump for all of his economic challenges. "To pin that on this administration, I don't think is a fair assessment," he said.

He pointed to cumbersome regulations as well as the rising cost of machinery and fertiliser - trends that began before Trump returned to the White House.

Mannon, who returned to her native Nebraska and bought the ranch after a career in banking, believes the agricultural industry will show its feelings at the midterms.

But like many around here, she prefers not to engage in too much political debate.

That is not a problem for her friend and nearby rancher Jim Jenkins. A former independent senatorial candidate, Jenkins is fiercely proud of Nebraska agriculture and his own ranch, which is on land his family homesteaded more than 150 years ago.

Jenkins has been so incensed by the policies he feels are harming Nebraska's agricultural industry that he wrote an opinion article over the summer in an Omaha paper.

He has felt the squeeze personally too, citing high diesel, fertiliser, lumber and steel costs - everything from barbed wire to fence posts.

That has been compounded by "uncertainty" over what may happen next, he said, and what the next Trump announcement might mean for the industry.

"Those are the things that keep you up at night," the 69-year-old told BBC News.

An outspoken Trump critic who didn't vote for the president during any of his White House bids, Jenkins knows he is an outlier among his conservative neighbours. When Trump was first elected, Jenkins said he hoped he would turn out "to be a practical business guy".

But for many Trump-supporting farmers and ranchers, the president's decisions - even when they hit them economically - deserve the benefit of the doubt.

"We've all known this about Trump. He just kind of could be a little 'shoot, fire, aim,'" Wolfinger said. "I wish you could, you know, put the gun back and holster it and then think about it."

But, he said, "I think he's, for the most part, trying to run this country in the right direction".

Don Cantrell, whose grandfather started farming family land that now stretches to 12,000 acres, said he is still getting hit on diesel and admits the president "does some stupid things" and "says some stupid things".

But Cantrell believes Trump has been the "best president overall". His establishment of DOGE - the Department of Government Efficiency - for example, was exactly what he felt the country needed.

"Let's cut government waste," he said. "There's so much waste."

Trump also maintains stances on social issues - like abortion and praising Christianity - that align with many Nebraskan voters' personal convictions.

"I think, in general, if you're conservative in this country, you're going to vote conservative," Wolfinger said.

Don Batie, 67, agrees: "There's a lot of other issues besides agriculture."

Batie retired from farming last year for a combination of personal and economic reasons. The corn and soybean farmer watched as prices fell from $7 a bushel for corn in early 2022 to just $4.29 three years later.

But costs have not gone down, he said, with tariffs and inflation contributing to his bottom line. As a result, he has had to abandon his longtime dream of passing on the 400-acre farm he owns to his daughter.

"It just wasn't going to work now," he said, sitting at the dining room table in the home he grew up in.

He only came to that realisation within the past year after crunching the numbers.

"I knew things hadn't been good," he said. "But when I started working on the numbers… I was like, 'This is going to be bad.'"

Batie voted for Trump in 2016 and again in the primary - but not in 2024, because he was disappointed with his policies. He said he had heard similar dissatisfaction throughout the state.

"They're still strong Republicans," he said of those people."But they're not a Trump supporter anymore."

On a rainy Thursday in Broken Bow, buyers clad in cowboy hats, plaid shirts and denim gathered for the regular indoor cattle auction.

Calves still need to be bought and sold, and ranch operations - many multi-generational - don not pause for politics.

Across the train tracks, past feed and hardware stores, Yvette Mannon summed up Nebraskans' resilience and fortitude.

"People in agriculture are eternal optimists," she said "Otherwise we wouldn't get in it."

items.title: Mourners killed by Kenya police at ex-PM's national farewell not part of violence, BBC finds
items.summary: After analysing 1,500 videos and images of the Raila Odinga memorial, Africa Eye finds that those killed were far from the scuffles.
items.content:
Three mourners killed when Kenyan police opened fire at a national farewell for former Prime Minister Raila Odinga were not involved in a clash that sparked gunfire, a BBC Africa Eye investigation has found.

During an event held last October for people to pay their respects to Odinga, three people were shot dead after mourners attempted to gain access to the VIP section of Nairobi's Kasarani Stadium by force.

BBC analysis from inside the stadium shows the victims were each between at least 60m (197 ft) and 160m from the scuffles.

Kenya's Interior Minister Kipchumba Murkomen told the BBC that the police action had been "restrained" after the crowd starting throwing stones.

In footage analysed by the BBC, it is clear that objects, including plastic chairs, are thrown, but we have no evidence that they included stones.

The BBC went through more than 1,500 images and videos to establish the location of those killed in the stadium on 16 October 2025, and also spoke to some of their relatives.

Forensic analysis by the BBC suggests an elite police unit responsible for protecting the president may have fired the fatal shots.

Kenya's longest serving opposition leader and former prime minister died the previous day while receiving medical treatment in India. He was one of the country's most influential political figures.

A year on, Kenya's police watchdog, the Independent Policing Oversight Authority (IPOA), is still investigating the deaths and police response and no-one has been held to account.

The interior minister defended the police by saying they had been under "so much pressure" after working for many hours non-stop and had been deployed to a new venue at the last minute.

"The investigations are being done by an independent police oversight authority, we believe that their findings will help us take appropriate legal action," Murkomen said.

Responding to questions about the conduct of police he said: "I don't think… somebody [was] sitting there and saying: 'Shoot now'. It is the judgment of the police officer at the spur of the moment."

Yvonne Akinyi, who husband was among those killed told the BBC: "The people who we look at to protect us, these are the people that cause us this pain. These are the people that make us to become young widows in this country, young orphans in this county," she said.

Odinga's death at 80 prompted an outpouring of grief across Kenya. Thousands gathered at Nairobi's Jomo Kenyatta International Airport as his body was flown home.

The body had originally been due to lie in state at parliament, but the scale of the crowds and fears of a security breach forced a last-minute change of venue to Kasarani Stadium. Officials say they had little time to secure the 48,000-capacity venue, and thousands spilled onto the pitch and into the stands unchecked.

After several hours of waiting to see the coffin in 30C heat with no public address system for official updates, a small section of the crowd began throwing objects, including plastic chairs, at officers guarding the VIP pavilion. Police fired live rounds as mourners pushed toward the pavilion. Footage from elsewhere in the stadium shows the crowd remained largely peaceful.

BBC Africa Eye investigates the killing of three mourners at Raila Odinga’s national farewell

One of them was Evans Kiche, a 40 year-old-chef and father to seven children. BBC analysis shows he was around 60m from the confrontation when he was killed by a gunshot wound to the head.

The two other mourners killed, Vincent Ogutu and Jidah Burka, were at least 160m away, in the opposite stands, far removed from the pavilion.

Autopsy reports confirm that Ogutu died from a gunshot wound to the chest and 42 year-old Burka was fatally shot in the head.

Piecing together a timeline of events, BBC Africa Eye identified at least eight police officers operating together, wearing tactical clothing and military camouflage. These officers carry assault rifles, with no visible insignia and faces covered.

Their uniforms and movements are consistent with a layer of security assigned to President William Ruto and other VIPs before and after the shooting. At least three officers of this unit appear to fire their weapons.

The BBC identified three of them as part of an elite police unit responsible for presidential protection.

The BBC cannot establish which bullets killed each victim, and cannot rule out other officers firing inside the stadium.

Kenya's National Police Service told the BBC: "There are huge lessons picked from the day's events," which had "formed a fundamental learning curve for a better, more professional application in the future." The IPOA did not respond to a request for comment.

Ogutu, a 36-year-old father of three, hadn't planned to go to Kasarani, his wife told the BBC. He was in central Nairobi on the morning of 16 October with friends when they saw the crowds heading to the stadium and decided to join.

His widow Yvonne Akinyi described how the killing upended their family, saying their children were now orphans.

As she prepares to mark a year since her husband's death, Akinyi is no closer to understanding why he died while paying his respects at an event organised by the government.

"I will just try to be that strong woman. Very strong. But deep inside there is a hole," she said.

"It is very painful because sometimes you just sit down and ask yourself. At Kasarani there were so many people, so many of them. Why him."
